Supply-Agriculture
DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Administration branch-
1. Departmental administration including the national co-ordinating committee on agricultural services, $1,003,000.

Mr. Chairman, as a result of one of those last minute changes in the order of business to which we are becoming accustomed now I find myself in a position where I can complete the statement I began a week ago last Wednesday, I think it was, when the Minister of Agriculture introduced his estimates in the committee.
At that time I was commenting on an official visit made by the minister to Saskatchewan where he spoke to the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. This was an official visit as we learned, Mr. Chairman, and on that occasion the minister made certain important proposals. But we were told shortly after they were made, though the audience itself was not told during the minister's speech, that these proposals were made by the minister in his personal capacity on an official visit, and in that sense the minister's proposals as official proposals or official suggestions or whatever you want to call them were repudiated by the Prime Minister. At the time I characterized this procedure as ridiculous, as indeed it was.
1 think you could use the same expression, Mr. Chairman, to characterize the proposal which was made to the effect that the producers should at this date share in the credit risk on deals for wheat sales made with foreign powers, particularly China, when those arrangements were made at a time by the government when the producers were told that the government would take all the risk. When a proposal is made to have an arrangement changed in a way which would repudiate the undertaking previously given, that is also, Mr. Chairman, worthy of condemnation.
One wonders why, when there was a credit risk involved of $170 million-I believe that was the figure-concerning which the producers were told they would bear no share of the risk, that stand should be questioned by the government now when the risk is $190 million. This is something we would like to hear about later when the minister completes his statement to the committee. As far as the suggestion of the producers sharing the risk with the government on future deals is concerned, no doubt the farmers and farm organizations will themselves give whatever consideration is required to any suggestion of that kind. However, they may be confused, Mr. Chairman, in that consideration by the fact that they do not know now whether the

suggestion put forward by the minister was for present arrangements or future arrangements, or whether it was put forward by the minister in his personal capacity and has been repudiated by the government.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the stand we have taken in regard to this particular matter does not represent, as I said the other day to the committee, any change of position on our part in regard to the desirability, especially at this time, of sales of agricultural commodities on credit, particularly because of the amount of wheat sales involved. Our position in this regard is quite clear. We began the sales of agricultural commodities on credit back in 1955. It is interesting to recall, and I mentioned this the other day without going into the details. At that time the first credit wheat deal was brought before parliament in 1955; an arrangement had been made with the government of Poland. The Conservative leader of the opposition of that day, Mr. Drew, moved the adjournment of the house to call attention to this credit deal with a communist country, Poland. He moved the adjournment of the house to deal with this as a matter of immediate and urgent public concern because, as he said, the negotiations were not yet completed. He went on to say in his motion that if gifts or quasi gifts-he was referring to this credit deal-are to be made to foreign countries they should be made to friendly powers as part of the general strengthening of democracy. This was the stand taken by the leader of the Conservative opposition at that time.
While we may approve of credit deals, as not only necessary and desirable under present circumstances, it is of course clear as I pointed out before that special care should be taken in regard to credit deals with communist countries. There is no better illustration of the necessity for care in these matters than the deal which has been negotiated, the arrangement or whatever you wish to call it, by the wheat board with the communist government of China, to cover the sale of wheat on credit to that country.
The other day in this house, Mr. Chairman, when this matter came up in connection with the conflict going on now between India and communist China, the Prime Minister said it would be undesirable in the circumstances as they existed to break the contract of sale with communist China. After the Prime Minister made that statement the Minister of Agriculture himself, in answer to a question, said there was no contract between the government and communist China-
No, between the wheat board and communist China; that is where the contract is.

There is, of course, Mr. Chairman, an arrangement, agreement, contract or whatever you wish to call it, between the wheat board and communist China. I should like to emphasize that because the Prime Minister has confirmed the situation. The contract, arrangement or deal is between the wheat board and the communist government of China, which makes it even more surprising that the Minister of Agriculture had to go all the way to Hong Kong to sign some kind of letter after the contract had been signed between the wheat board and communist China.
What we have, of course, is an agreement with communist China in the form-well, we do not know what form it is in; we have not been able to see it. It may be a letter of intent. It was to run, it has been stated-and perhaps the minister will confirm or deny this when he rises to speak-to December, 1963. I have heard the date referred to as December, 1963. This arrangement can of course be broken off, so I am informed-and I think the minister himself has already indicated this-at any time by either party to the agreement. It can be broken off if the Chinese communist government is not in a position to finance further purchases within the agreement; it can be broken off if Canada is not in a position to supply further quantities within the agreement, though fortunately that is not a contingency which is likely to arise. Or perhaps there is some escape clause in the agreement covering war, emergency, or something of that kind. In any event, it is clear that a contract for a specific sale within the agreement has to be made separately in the case of each amount.
We do not know how many of those arrangements have been made. We hear reports in the press that members of the wheat board are now in Hong Kong negotiating at this time, in the present circumstances, further sales within the agreement; further contracts, if you like. These negotiations are now going on, according to the press. Perhaps the minister will have something to say about that when he speaks again in this debate. No doubt if and when these arrangements for additional amounts come to a successful conclusion in Hong Kong and the contract is signed by the representative of the wheat board, the minister will then hurry off to Hong Kong to take some ex post facto part in the arrangement.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the Leader of the Opposition would permit a question.
Sit down.

I would like to ask the Leader of the Opposition whether he or his

party was against credit sales to China, and is he against them under the circumstances which exist today?

Mr. Chairman, all the hon. member has to do is read Hansard when I talked about this matter the other day. I think the hon. gentleman knows how to read, and if so he can read Hansard of a week ago when I put on the record the statement I made a year ago in regard to these China wheat arrangements. Indeed, before these arrangements were made the position of the Liberal party was on record, at a time when we were criticized by the Conservative party for making our position clear, with regard to selling foodstuffs to Asian countries, irrespective of the form of government in those countries. Perhaps my hon. friend is one of those who criticized us at the time we made our position clear.
The Minister of Agriculture made another proposal in Regina, whether in an official or personal capacity will be cleared up no doubt, in due course. That was that the pools might provide a kind of export agency to assist in the sale of wheat, an objective, of course, which we all support.
Oh, oh.

I said the objective of exporting wheat is one that every hon. member of the house supports, and the minister is not on very difficult grounds when he puts that forward. The minister also put forward the proposal that the pools set up some kind of export agency to facilitate export. Perhaps the minister knows-and if he does not know he should-that the three pools have been studying and examining this possibility for many months now and this is nothing new to them at all. In due course, no doubt, the pools will tell the minister how they feel about a proposal of this kind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Then why was it ridiculous when it was made, as far as you were concerned?

I have already said, for the Minister of Agriculture to go to Regina in an official capacity and make a personal statement which was repudiated by the Prime Minister the next day is a ridiculous procedure; and so it is. I have already said, and repeated today, for the Minister of Agriculture to make a proposal to the producers of wheat that they share in the risks of credit sales, when they were told six months ago they would not have to share in the risks at all, is also a ridiculous procedure. For the minister to put forward the proposal that the pools set up some export agency, when the pools themselves have been considering this for many months, perhaps is

Supply-Agriculture
not ridiculous but is not one likely to commend itself as a new and impressive proposal to those to whom he was talking.
Mr. Chairman, in recent months and recent weeks, and indeed in recent days, some of the buoyant optimism of the Minister of Agriculture in regard to our prospects for future export sales seems to have disappeared. According to the minister's recent speeches, his outlook on these matters seems somehow to have changed. Perhaps that is because he has had to recognize that the situation today has indeed changed. Across the landscape there is now visible what will probably be one of the biggest of bursting balloons when the present situation is compared with what the minister said would be the situation in this field about six months or so ago.
Only a few months ago, according to the minister and his supporters, everything was wonderful, and we had the minister largely to thank for this. That was the story which was told, particularly to the western farmers. Even when the Minister of Agriculture was appearing on television to say how wonderful things were, even after the election of June 20, at the very time the cabinet was deciding on an emergency program, on surcharges and on the highest cost of money we have ever had in this country.
During the election when these rosy stories were being related to the people of Canada by the minister and his supporters, the minister also said that the $40 million in acreage payments was to be made into a permanent policy, a permanent subsidy. Perhaps when the minister rises to speak he will tell us what has happened to that exciting promise. At that time we on this side of the chamber put forward, in place of an acreage payment as a subsidy, a guaranteed floor price for wheat through a consumer subsidy. When that proposal was put forward the minister saw fit to sneer at it as being quite inadequate; perhaps I can use the word again, as ridiculous. He preferred, so he said, the acreage payment proposal, made on a hit or miss basis according to the exigencies of the political situation at any particular time.
But surely, Mr. Chairman, it would be far better and would have provided far greater security to the producers to have a system of assistance based on long term, sound principles, a system of support prices, of floor prices and, in the case of wheat-as we put forward-a floor price which would be maintained by consumer subsidies. This proposal would have ensured, if it had been carried into effect for the life of the international wheat agreement, that the wheat producers of this country would receive no less than $2 a bushel for their wheat.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: On what wheat?
That was to be the floor price-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: On what wheat?

No. 1 northern. The minister knows that. The farmer will know and be able to consider the relative advantages and disadvantages of those two proposals, the government's proposal for acreage payments on a hit or miss basis and our proposal of a guaranteed floor price of $2. And, incidentally, we have put that forward not in a speech by any member of our party in his personal capacity but as official policy. When that policy was announced the minister scoffed at it and misrepresented it in a way which, indeed, made it sound ridiculous because, to quote him, he said "Why, the Leader of the Opposition promises only $2 a bushel for the next three years?" Then again, he said:
The man-
And I was the man.
-promises the western farmers less than they are now getting.
That is true.

That was not true at all. That is a complete misrepresentation. The minister should know the difference between a floor price and a market price.
But let that pass. What did the minister say about the market price at that time? On June 16 at Weyburn, Saskatchewan, according to the Leader-Post the hon. gentleman said the price would go to $2.19, that there was almost no chance of the price dropping. He repeated his appeal to the farmers at that time-and it was a very attractive appeal- to grow all the corn they could. We shall sell it, he said.
Hear, hear.

I shall come to that in a minute. Well, what is the price now, the price that had no chance of dropping? At the moment I believe it is just under $1.97 and it will be less, if the minister has his way, by the amount of the credit insurance program the farmer would have to pay if that proposal were adopted. Take the price of Durum wheat. During the election campaign it was $2.50 a bushel and the minister again said "Grow all you can; we will sell it." Then on August 1 the price was dropped from $2.50 to $1.50.
Certainly the situation now is not as rosy as the minister used to claim credit for. Perhaps this is one reason for the changed character of the hon. gentleman's recent statements. There are other aspects of agriculture

which are not as rosy as the minister indicated they were. There is the premium on grade A hogs, cut in half since the election, from $3 to $2. Then there is the butter situation. Having talked about this situation at the Ottawa conference this week the minister will no doubt tell the committee what he intends to do about it, as well as about the problems of the dairy industry generally which seem to have aroused a good deal of anxiety in the hon. gentleman's mind-and understandably so, with the amount of butter in the possession of the government now running to about 250 million.
I believe that as of September 29, some 234 million pounds of butter or butter oil was held. The cost for storage of this butter in 1961, for one year alone, was almost $4 million.
This represents a difficult problem, and the minister will no doubt tell us what he intends to do about it. Perhaps he intends to adopt an entirely different approach to this question, because he is reported as having said in Kitchener on May 25, during the election campaign, that subsidized agriculture is on the way out. If so he will no doubt inform the committee by what method he intends to replace the assistance which producers have been getting from what he calls subsidized agriculture. "It is all becoming very difficult now" says the minister. I wonder whether he is still advising producers, as he used to, to "Grow all you can and we will sell it". No longer, now, does he claim the only problem before us is how we are going to fill our orders, as he used to say some months ago.
What has happened? Let us see what the minister himself had to say about it in his Regina speech. On page 4 of the text of that speech he said:
It is clear we are lacing a period of much greater competition for export markets.
Certainly that is true. Then on page 5 he says:
We cannot afford to remain aloof from credit sales without facing up to the economic problems associated with the lower level of exports which would otherwise result.
We on this side have been pointing this out for a long time, emphasizing both the necessity and the risk attached to credit sales; pointing out the danger when too high a proportion of our exports is sold for credit and too low a proportion is sold for cash. Is the minister now aware of this danger attaching to the over-extension of credit and the demand for more and easier credit by some customers on whom we have become more and more dependent? I am thinking, of course, of communist China.
Supp ly-A griculture
In regard to wheat-and this has a bearing on what I have been saying-we may at times think too much about the conventional wheat exporters against whom we have to compete, and have been competing for many years, and not enough about those countries which generally produce wheat only for their own consumption but which in recent years have begun to enter world markets as important exporters. The best example of this at the present time is France. This year France is harvesting almost as big a crop of wheat as the big crop we have harvested in Canada, almost 500 million bushels. Too many people think of France as an importer of wheat. Of that 500 million bushels there will be available for export from France 176 million bushels, of which quantity France has already sold a total of 147 million bushels. That is the kind of thing which makes our position difficult, and it is the kind of situation which should be brought to the attention of the producers and exporters, as the minister himself seems now to be doing. On page 6 of his Regina statement the hon. gentleman says:
Selling conditions will be highly competitive in the months ahead and it will require an extraordinarily intensive sales effort to achieve an export level much in excess of 300 million bushels.
And he adds in this speech:
If we don't do that we shall be in trouble.
But what had the minister been saying only a few months earlier? The record is a fantastic one of misleading and exaggerated optimism in the light of what has happened since that day. On December 16, 1961, according to the Leader-Post, the minister said at Radville in Saskatchewan:
I am asking you to produce 500 million bushels a year-150 million for domestic consumption and 350 million for export.
The average production for the last four years, I think, has been about 312 million bushels. Last spring, while the farmers were putting in their crops on the eve of the election campaign, the hon. gentleman was even more cheerful. As reported in the Globe and Mail of April 30, 1962, after referring to a statement released by his department he-
*-urged grain producers to grow every bushel of wheat, oats and barley they can to meet requirements of 1.1 billion bushels this year.
He told them:
Employ every proved technique to conserve moisture and increase your production with complete confidence that there will be hungry markets, good prices and more space available for your grain in country elevators than at any time in the past 10 years.
Would the minister confirm that now as an estimate for the future? On June 6 the

Supply-Agriculture
minister was even more exuberant. At Wey-burn, according to the Regina Leader-Post, he estimated that this year 375 million bushels would be sold. Would the minister confirm that estimate now?
Three hundred million?

Three hundred and seventy five million. Then at Wetaskiwin on June 12-we are getting close to the election date- according to the Edmonton Journal he said this, which should be compared to the advice he gave to farmers in Regina a few days ago. The Edmonton Journal reports the minister's statement on June 12 in this way. The heading is "Hamilton says government will sell every bushel", and the report goes on:
We say to the farmers-"You fellows grow wheat and we can sell every bushel of it for you, 600 million bushels if you have it"-
Does the minister still confirm that prediction of sales, "600 million bushels if you have it"? The report continues:
Allegations that the Canadian wheat board had sold wheat to China before he arrived in Hong Kong to conclude the deal were described by Mr. Hamilton as "nonsense"-
Well, Mr. Chairman, those were the statements of the minister in the months preceding the election and during the election campaign, which are to be compared with what he said in Regina the other day and the statements he has made in this house.
Let us see from the figures what progress we are making to fulfil the rosy predictions of the minister that if the farmers produced
600	million bushels the government would sell 600 million bushels. This year we have had a good crop, 558 million bushels compared to 283 million bushels last year. Up to the present, according to the official figures issued a couple of weeks ago, the farmers marketed over 124 million as compared with 86 million for the same period last year. That means that wheat on the farms a couple of weeks ago amounted to some 434 million bushels, compared with 197 million bushels at the same time a year ago. With a visible supply of 361 million bushels, we get a total wheat supply as at the beginning of November of 795 million bushels, compared with
601	million bushels at the same period last year.
The total wheat supply at the end of the crop year was 396 million bushels; that was our carryover. To reach this level during the present crop year we are going to have to sell 194 million bushels more than we did between November 1 and July 31 last year. Since there are only 39 weeks left, that means that we must dispose of an additional 5 million bushels of wheat per week over last year. As there is not likely to be any appreciable change in domestic consumption,

that means that we must export 5 million bushels more per week than we did last year, or roughly three times as much as we did in the week ending October 31. But overseas clearances of wheat in the period August 1-October 31 are running 21 million bushels behind the same period last year. In the light of that fact, I wonder if the minister will confirm his earlier glowing predictions.
Mr. Chairman, there is one other matter I want to deal with. I will not do so in great detail, though it is a matter of such importance to our agriculture, indeed to all our producers, because it is worthy of a separate discussion in this house, and I hope it will soon receive that kind of consideration and discussion. It concerns developments in the European common market, and their possible effect on our agricultural producers. It is quite clear, of course, that whether the United Kingdom becomes a member of the European common market or whether it does not succeed in becoming a member of the European common market, European progress in the field of trade and tariff unification will have an important effect on our agricultural exports. It is surely equally clear that the government should be taking every possible step in every possible way by continuous negotiations at the highest possible level to ensure that these developments will take place with a minimum of damage to our agricultural producers.
Other countries appreciate that point in connection with their own producers. The secretary of agriculture in the United States is over in Europe now taking part in negotiations with the common market, and in Geneva at GATT, and no doubt also at the meetings of O.E.C.D., which I believe is to discuss these matters next week. The meeting of GATT is still going on-it will probably conclude shortly-among officials representing a good many governments at the ministerial level. But Canada is not represented. At the O.E.C.D. meetings we are also to be represented. That meeting will no doubt discuss economic relationships with the European common market and GATT; Canada and the United States, as I say, are to be represented at the O.E.C.D. meeting and will be taking part in these important discussions.
At that meeting we are to be represented not by the Minister of Agriculture, not by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, not by the Minister of Finance, but by the Minister of Justice. Surely nothing could be of greater importance to our economic wellbeing, both now and in the future, than to have Canada take an active and immediate ministerial part in every negotiation now going on or which could be initiated by it, and which concerns these developments in Geneva,

Brussels and Paris. Believe me, Mr. Chairman, in these negotiations between the United States and the European common market, whether the United Kingdom goes into the market or not we will not be given a tree ride through the operation of the most favoured nation clause. If we are going to make these developments work to the advantage, rather than to the damage, of Canada, we should be active in initiating negotiations on our own behalf at the highest political level and at the earliest possible moment.
In so far as the accession of the United Kingdom to the common market is concerned, if we in Canada try to lay down conditions far beyond those which are required for the legitimate protection of our own interests- and we certainly have to protect them-but which are designed to make it more difficult for the United Kingdom to join the common market, we will be taking on a very heavy responsibility indeed. If the impression created in some quarters is of a United Kingdom government fighting to get into the European common market at any price, the impression has also been created in many quarters of a Canadian government fighting to keep the United Kingdom out of the European common market.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are completely out of order.
That is completely false, and the hon. gentleman knows it.

The Prime Minister says that is completely false, and that I know it. Well, I will let the record show how false it is, from the Accra conference right on down to the last comonwealth prime ministers' conference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Would the Leader of the Opposition permit a question?
Sit down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Does he consider that the recent declaration of the United States secretary of agriculture constitutes whimpering in face of the European common market?

I am very glad indeed that the hon. member has brought that up, because it confirms exactly what I have been saying. From the very beginning the United States has shown a sympathetic understanding of the United Kingdom effort to get into the common market. The United States has also passed through congress a trade expansion program which it is using to negotiate with the common market. Having taken this position in principle, and having not whined and objected to these developments from the sidelines, the
Supply-Agriculture
United States has now sent its secretary of agriculture to Europe to negotiate the terms on which the United States can protect its own interests. And what are we doing in that connection?
That is the way in which a wise government would proceed, to having understood the importance of these great developments which are bringing Europe together and which I hope will bring Europe across the Atlantic, and, having created that sympathetic understanding of what is going on, then to fight to protect our own trading interests within the ambit of that understanding. That is the way in which these things should be done, instead of trying to create the impression, at Accra and subsequently, that it is a matter of commonwealth or common market. Believe me, Mr. Chairman, our agricultural producers will not benefit if that alternative is the only one facing them, the commonwealth or the common market with Great Britain going into the common market or Great Britain staying out of the common market.
Moreover, the British are determined that such will not be the alternative, and they have their own producers in mind when they take that position. Mr. George Brown, the deputy leader of the Labour party in the House of Commons, in a debate on this matter had this to say on November 19, and I quote from British Hansard:
If these negotiations failed-
That is the negotiations for United Kingdom entry into the common market.
-they had better take note of the fact that there would be a question mark over the future of the community.
He is talking about the Six when he says "they".
They (the Six) must understand that we do not have to break our pledges to meet the future. It could be met one way or another but going into an enlarged community would be much the better way to meet it.
Then on October 29, the Prime Minister himself, Mr. Macmillan, said this-repeating what he has said many times previously- at the Conservative party conference:
I am persuaded that the commonwealth is complementary and not an alternative to the consolidation of Europe.
And Mr. Butler, his deputy, said at the same conference:
This is emphatically not a choice between the commonwealth and Europe. Our objective is to give Britain greater strength in order to help the commonwealth.
Whatever happens, the results will be important for the agricultural producers of this

Supply-Agriculture
country. Whatever happens, it is not likely that the old system of commonwealth preferences on which we have built up so much of our agricultural production in this country in the past-and we all know that-will be retained intact; whether Great Britain enters the common market or not. Any effort to try to impress on our producers that it is possible to maintain intact commonwealth preferences, whatever happens, is doomed to failure. As Right Hon. Mr. Butler himself said when he was speaking on October 29:
I should say from a whole life's experience in agriculture that there probably is a need for a change in our present system anyway.
We had better accept that fact, especially when it was confirmed by the secretary of state for commonwealth relations, Right Hon. Duncan Sandys, at the same conference, speaking on the same platform, when he said this, and these are words that are important:
Whether we join the common market or not our system of free entry and preferences will in any case have to be reviewed to relate to the altered conditions of today.
It is quite clear, Mr. Chairman, that changes are going to take place whatever happens to the British application to join the common market, that these changes are going to have an effect on the agricultural producers in this country. This government should be adopting policies which will help to adapt our producers to these changes. There are going to be immediate changes, whatever happens; there are going to be immediate difficulties.
However, there will be long range advantages, I am sure, to set against these immediate disadvantages. Surely as a government and as a parliament our main objective should be to do what we can to put into effect the kind of policies which will enable Canada to utilize the long range advantages; to do what we can to ensure that the European common market is built up with the United Kingdom in or with the United Kingdom out, as an outward looking organization with a minimum of obstruction to trade between itself and the outer world. If it is expansionist and if it is outward looking we can gain a great deal for agricultural producers from this development. Otherwise, of course, we shall have trouble.
It seems to me that a very wise stand has been taken in this matter by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and I quote from the president of the federation on January 5, 1962, when, in speaking for the federation, Mr. Hannam said this:
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has always looked upon the development of the European common market as being, in principle, a

policy of statesmanship and wisdom. It has recognized the dangers of the agricultural policies of the Six taking a protectionist turn that could jeopardize our markets in some commodities. But it has believed that the only right lies in fully acknowledging the rightness of the common market concept, and bending our energies through consultation, agreement, and enlightened trade policy on our part, toward turning to our benefit the trade potential which should be opened up by an economically united, prosperous and expanding Europe.
That is the right approach to these developments which are taking place in Europe. That is the approach which will help the agricultural producers and other producers in this country. That is the approach that should be taken by this government. However, it is the approach that up to the present time has not been taken by this government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: May I ask a further question?
Sit down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We should like to understand the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition, and if I may do so, I should like to ask him a question. He has indicated that he seems to be in support of the United States stand. Is he advocating that we threaten reprisals on the European common market, as the Americans have done?

No, I am not advocating any such course of reprisals. That course, of course, would not be very sensible. What I am advocating is this. When the United States trade expansion program was being developed, I say that Canada should have associated herself with that program from the beginning so that the kind of approach which is now being made unilaterally by the United States at Geneva and at Brussels on the ministerial level could have been made by Canada and the United States together. Indeed, if Canada had shown any interest in the trade expansion program in Washington at the beginning, the act of congress embodying that program could have been altered to have included important Canadian products in it among those for which the United States would have received power to remove the duty completely. At that time Canada showed no interest in that program. Canada showed a rather standoffish and suspicious attitude at that time. Now when the U.S. secretary of agriculture is over there speaking for his country in these negotiations which are taking place, who is over there speaking for Canada?
I have been talking mostly about western agriculture especially grain production, but of course that is not the only aspect of the agricultural industry which will be considered in the discussion of the estimates. Indeed, other sectors of the agricultural industry are

now, in terms of dollar production value, even more important than grain. An answer was given the other day to a question in the House of Commons, it can be found at page 752 of Hansard, which answer gives some very striking information about the relative importance in the last year, in terms of dollar production and dollar value, of the various segments of the agricultural industry. It shows that the total gross value of grain production in 1961 was $308,792,000. That value, incidentally, in 1961 was less than half the value of grain production in 1960. The total value of fruit and vegetable production was $183 million; that of other field crops, $259 million. But the total gross value of livestock production in this country in 1961 was over $1 billion. The total gross value of dairy products in that year was $567 million and of poultry products $317 million. The total gross value of all agricultural production in 1961 was $2,706 million compared with $2,980 million in the previous year, 1960.
There are other very important aspects of this industry, therefore, which will have to be considered in the discussion of these estimates. My colleagues on this side will be very glad to bring up questions of particular importance to these other segments. Meanwhile we are looking forward to the Minister of Agriculture continuing his statement, which he was not able to complete the other day. Perhaps in that statement he will be able to deal with some of the points I have raised and to reconcile the extravagant, exaggerated, optimistic claims he made during the election campaign, especially about exports of wheat, with the situation confronting us today which he referred to in his speech in Regina where, on an official mission, he gave a personal evaluation of the position.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak in this debate I would preface my remarks by saying that agriculture is still the basic industry of Canada. Tremendous strides have been taken in the production of all types of agricultural produce. If effective markets could be provided both at home and abroad our farmers could then be told to increase their production as much as possible and with the greatest possible speed. From this we understand that the real problem of agriculture today is one of distribution. This is the most urgent and greatest need of the industry.
The Canadian farmer is an individualist. He does not want nor does he look for charity or welfare. He does not want another segment of our economy to bear the responsibility of subsidizing him. All that he asks
Supp ly-A griculture
is a chance to sell his products at a reasonable price and with the co-operation of government at the different levels and with his own organizations, in working out his other problems. This does not apply just to the western wheat farmer but also applies to the farmer who grows fruit or potatoes in the maritimes or dairy products or feed grain, whatever it may be, in central Canada.
In dealing with the problems of the farmer I think we can only do so effectively if we look at them from the whole aspect. From my personal knowledge of farmers, no matter in what part of Canada they live, I believe they expect from their national government a policy that is equitable and fair to all regardless of the area of Canada in which they happen to be operating.
The response of the leader of the official opposition to the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture is one which arouses a great deal of interest. It would almost seem that the apparent agricultural spokesman of his party has fallen from grace. I do not even see him present today. However, to be replaced by his own leader must give the hon. member for Assiniboia at least some consolation. I am not sure whether the western farmers will be too convinced, after learning what the Leader of the Opposition has said, that he knows any more about the agricultural problems of the western farmer than he knew before. However, what the leader of the official opposition faced was one of the most questionable policies of the government in the sale of grains, but he went to incredible lengths- he did so the other day and he has done so today-to put on record the fact that not only did the Liberal party support trade on credit with red China but that the idea of communist trade was solely theirs in the first place.
There is even evidence to think that in the interval since his last contribution to this debate he has perhaps changed some of the opinions that he expressed then. He has made a great deal of the speech that the Minister of Agriculture made not too long ago in Saskatchewan. While I do not agree with many of the policies that the Minister of Agriculture has laid down and practised during his years in office, I believe when the records of this government find their way into history no one will be able to accuse the minister of not working and working hard for the farmers of Canada.
The minister asked for the help of the western farmers in carrying the risk of credit selling of agricultural produce, particularly wheat. While I respect the honesty and sincerity with which this request was made, I do not believe it was politically or otherwise

Supp ly-A griculture
sound. While we give the minister credit for the fact that his party has the largest minority in this house because of his efforts on behalf of the western farmer, I would caution him that he can lose that support just as quickly by proposing such alternatives to the western farmer who, I am quite convinced, does not feel it is his responsibility to bear the possible loss that may result from default of payments in such sales.
However, I think the request for assistance in the sale of our agricultural products is a good suggestion. The wider you can spread the responsibility of trying to ease our problem of distribution, the better it is for all concerned. I would simply say that this is good provided that any help the U.G.G. or the pools can give in this regard is that of a salesman rather than that of selling agencies. I think this principle applies not only to the western farmer but also to every aspect of our Canadian economy.
It is interesting in this regard that the sale of our agricultural products is, I believe, one of the most important problems facing us today, and I think it is a responsibility of this house of minorities to try together to work out the problem in such a way that we can sell the agricultural products that we produce. What we must comprehend is simply this, that the greatest revolution in the world's history is taking place today, the revolution of humanity against the tyranny of hunger and want. Because this is true, the greatest weapon we have in our hands is the weapon of surplus food, for the lack of which thousands in the world are dying.
There are today approximately one billion children living in the world. On the basis of the statistics supplied through the various agencies of the United Nations and the governments of the world, it is estimated that one half of those children will never reach adulthood simply because they do not have enough to eat to keep body and soul together. Therefore, so far as I am concerned, so far as we are concerned here, so far as the farmers are concerned, so far as those who are concerned with the preservation of world peace and the development of the world's resources for the progress of mankind, the greatest threat before us today is the threat of hunger.
On the converse side of this, the most potent weapon we have in Canada is our food surplus.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

One day I heard the hon. member say it is better to be fed than red.

I have also heard him criticize the wheat sales to communist China. Since we are on that subject now, how does he reconcile these two statements?

If the hon. member for Bow River will just be patient for a few minutes he will have that answer.
The most important job facing the world today is to feed the hungry. There is no use talking about democracy and free elections to people with empty bellies. They do not ask, when do we vote? The most burning question to them is, when do we eat? Without freedom from hunger there is no freedom. The chief question, therefore, confronting our generation is not how many rockets we can send to the moon, not how we can reduce the cost of death-dealing missiles, but rather whether men can learn to live together on this planet and, in living together, have enough to meet their physical needs. The real issue at hand and the truth of the matter at this time, while we think peace, we talk peace, and we pray for peace, is that we are at war. We are in a war that is called a cold war. It is called a war of ideologies.
However, whatever name we give it, let us remember that this war is a war between two sides. One side says people shall be free and have an opportunity to have their needs met as we in the world can produce and as it is necessary to meet those needs. The other side says that man should serve the state and that man's needs are met as the state controls and dictates. So, whatever our policies are relating to whatever aspects of our economy or government or national life, we might consider that they must be geared to these facts. This is particularly true in the field of agriculture as it relates to the sale of our surplus food products.
I would love to hear the Minister of Agriculture say to the farmers of Canada, produce all you can because as long as there is a hungry mouth in the world we will see that the food is distributed. This is our collective responsibility. Let us remember, as we look at the world situation, that this war is not going to be settled by atomic missiles nor by the brute power of force. It is going to be settled by an economic offensive that is rapidly enveloping us today. The side that comes out the victor is going to be the side that can solve these economic problems in the best way to meet the needs of the hungry of the world.
It is for this reason that I point my finger at the Minister of Agriculture and say his policies, as they relate to the selling of wheat to communist countries, are without effect unless we have an external affairs policy that is integrated with his policies. You cannot have a proper trade policy unless it is

integrated as well. If we cannot have a defence policy that is related to this same picture, then we do not have any hope of winning this war.
It is for this reason I say to the government, unless you bring down a policy that springs from a coherent basic concept of the world's needs in relation to defence problems, to general trade, to agricultural trade, we will never meet our responsibilities in this cold war of which we are a part.
This integrated basic policy is what we need today. It is the type of leadership we expect and demand, not only as members of this house but on behalf of the people of Canada; because the peace and development of our civilization is something about which everyone is concerned. We are concerned with the preservation and extension of the free way of life that we have and which we prize so much in our own country.
Let us face this thing, therefore, for what it is. Behind it there is a moral issue, an issue that rests on the simple foundation of what is right and what is wrong. Two wrongs will never make a right. You cannot neutralize a greater wrong with a lesser one or vice versa. Until we can face these moral issues as we believe them to be, then we cannot succeed. Today part of the world is in slavery and part of it is free. A world so divided cannot exist for very long. Either one or the other must be eliminated. Democracies endeavour to do this by respecting individual rights, the freedom of individuals. The communists do this by denying individual rights and individual freedom. But the hour glass of time runs its relentless course and, as it runs, the difference between these two concepts becomes more acute. The ultimate survival of one will depend on its ability to satisfy the basic needs of mankind.
Let us remember, in relation to the trade offensive that reaches into our democratic nations from the communist countries, that the man behind this whole thing is a man by the name of Mikoyan, the U.S.S.R. first deputy premier. He is the man who directs the Russian economic aid program and the trade agreements which the communists are endeavouring to make with the uncommitted countries in an effort to win their allegiance. As a professional economist he is the front line general of the Russian cold war. On his resourcefulness may depend the final outcome of this, the cold war's decisive front. The weapons he uses are order blanks and unlimited credit.
In the struggle for men's minds the Russians have embarked on a new sales campaign to win converts to communism by offering trade agreements and credits which eastern businessmen cannot resist. We are
Supply-A griculture
faced with the same thing in our trade relationships today with communist China, as we realize that there has been a threat of war -it is still there-in the Himalayan mountain front of northern India. Let us remember that while this threat is still upon us in all its gravity, we have a Canadian delegation in Hong Kong trading and negotiating. This is the very country that has invaded a commonwealth nation.
Let us remember here also that last year, while we sold our wheat to communist China, communist China was selling its wheat to Russia to pay for the oil that is being used right now to transport Chinese troops across the mountains of Tibet. While we were selling our wheat to China, Russia was selling her wheat to Japan. The only difference was that while we sold it for credit, Russia sold it for cash. These are facts that cannot be denied. However, the trading agencies of the Soviet union, and indirectly those of all communist countries, are responsible to this gentleman who has so recently spent several weeks right in this hemisphere on our doorstep.
A stumbling block in the communist system is that every trade contract becomes a commercial treaty between governments, and in the event that a change is required, it is more involved than a simple commercial contract. Whether or not the Minister of Agriculture says the Canadian government has a contract with the communist government or not, this fact is true. The biggest advantage of the communist system is that trade agreements can be planned with a long range view in mind. Present losses may be balanced against gains in future years. There is the further factor that the communists can gear their economic policies with their political policies in a way that the democracies cannot do. A commercial loss may be compensated for by a political gain, in the bookkeeping of the communist. Therefore we find that while we try to justify the sale of our wheat to communist countries, we are providing a weapon for those communist countries to extend their tyranny to other peoples who are yet free.
I was interested to read the other day, as I am sure every hon. member of this house was, the remarks of a man who lived in China and knows what goes on there. He is no passing journalist; he is not one who passes through on a two weeks' excursion tour. He is a man who has lived there for several years. I am speaking of the ambassador of Denmark to the nation whose capital is Peking. I would like to quote

Supply-Agriculture
what he said as it was reported on November 15 in the Globe and Mail, the dateline being Athens:
"Not a grain of Canadian wheat has ever reached the starving masses of China. If the average Canadian only knew what ruthless purposes Canada's wheat shipments to Peking were serving, I doubt if a single shipment would have been allowed to go through" . ..
According to Mr. Bertelsen, Canada's much advertised grain shipments to China were exclusively used to bolster the communist regime. This the reds shrewdly achieved by distributing the wheat only to the armed forces, factory workers in certain essential industries and-
As he said, to other nations they were trying to influence. Then he said:
"I can assure you that the weary, haggard masses in China have never tasted a grain of Canadian wheat"-
He also said this:
"All of us western ambassadors in Peking made nearly identical reports to our respective governments stressing the consequences of such shipments"-
Coming back to the question of the hon. member from Bow River-

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question, in the interests of fairness. Would the hon. member read to the committee the statement in that article where the Danish ambassador to Peking stated that he was never allowed out of Peking?
I will not take time to read it now.
Oh, oh.
But he did say that, except for yearly excursions in which he took part.
How did he know about the wheat?

The record is there. I am sure he knows a lot more about it than some of us who have never been there, and others who have just passed through for a few days. I do not have that part of the clipping here. From Spokane comes another statement, date-lined the same day:
Canada sells wheat to China because it feels it is selling food to hungry people, not weapons to a hostile nation, a senior Canadian official said here.
The point is not whether we sell wheat to China but whether we are assisting in the extension of the communist world which has threatened to destroy us, and which will destroy us if we do not do something a little more effective than we are doing at the present time. It involves this also, from the other side; that there are millions of people just as hungry as the people of China, and starving in just as large numbers, who are on our side of this struggle and who would

like to continue to be on our side, and who, when they do succumb to the influence of communism, do so only because they have not had their needs met in the system under which they are living.
This is the moral issue that is involved. That is why I believe it is wrong to base our trade policies on this very mistaken impression of what the moral issue actually is. Our stand is not so much that selling wheat to communist China is wrong, if it reduces the number of hungry people. It is a fact that we are losing the battle for those who are still free and we are not fulfilling our obligations to them. It comes down to the fact that we in the western world do not make our economic system function for the benefit of the political scene, as the communists do. The communists can manipulate and work their economy in such a way that it furthers their political ends.
We have not time today to go into the background of this, but this is the basic difference in our approaches to trade. But let us remember this, Mr. Chairman; that behind this very issue is the fact that our economics have often dictated mistaken political philosophies, and until we can solve our economic problems we will never be able to straighten out our political standards.
I would like to quote from a statement by Major C. H. Douglas, the gentleman who first wrote on the principles of Social Credit as he saw the age of automation and abundance coming into being. In the book entitled "Program for the Third World War" published in 1943 he said this:
Now, once you have surrendered to materialism, it is quite true that economics precede politics, and dominate it. It is not in communism, fascism, or in the London school of economics Fabian society, or in a planned economy that we shall find the origins of what we are looking for. These are ostensibly political systems and derive from, rather than give birth to, economics. While this is obvious and axiomatic, it is not so obvious, although equally axiomatic, that the principle works both ways. That is as much as to say. if you can control economics, you can keep the business of getting a living the dominant factor of life, and so keep your control of politics-just that long and no longer.
Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member permit a question on this point?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, as long as it does not interfere with my time.
Would the hon. member make an unequivocal statement that the group he heads does not favour the sale of foodstuffs to red China and other communist countries?

The question the hon. member has asked must seemingly give some concern as far as the questioner is concerned. It is very easy to give an answer. As long as there

are hungry people on the free side of this struggle that I am talking about, who need our wheat and cannot get it, we are against the sale of wheat to communist China or any other such country,
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question?
As long as it is not using up my time, Mr. Chairman.

With regard to the remarks of the hon. member about those who are still free, is he suggesting that this government, which has already carried out a program of extensive aid under the Colombo plan, should extend and enlarge this, when the hon. member has stated previously time and again that he is against the subsidization of agriculture? Would not this be, in a sense, subsidizing agriculture further if we gave wheat to those people who are still free?

I will deal with this question in just a few minutes, Mr. Chairman. I would just like to say to the hon. member for Acadia that the only basis for the survival of our agricultural industry, including the family farm, is the setting up of a two price system that will allow us to export our surplus products. Unless we can do that we had better close up shop. This does not mean subsidies in the sense that we understand a subsidies program such as they have in the United States and which, whether we like it or not, is developing in our own midst. This two price system must be there to guarantee our farmers an equitable price to cover their cost of operation and to let us get our food products out to those people who do need them on the other side of the fence.
On the positive side, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say this to the Minister of Agriculture. Canda's long term policy must be to take action that will reduce, and not increase, world tension. This is not the whole responsibility of the minister, but it is his responsibility to the extent that he is the minister who lays down the agricultural trade policies that govern our struggle in this cold war. In all cases where totalitarian governments are involved we have no quarrel with the people who are the subjects of those governments, whether they be in China, Russia or any other place. Rather we sympathize with their position. We are opposed, however, to the extension of this type of government and policies which aid this type of government. We therefore believe that the proper test in connection with trade with all countries under a totalitarian form of government is "Does this trade give help
Supply-A griculture
to the people of the country, or does it further the aggressive designs of their government?" We cannot permit trade which helps fasten tyranny on other people, yet we must realize that refusal to trade in certain circumstances may lead to yet closer alignment of government with the communist powers, and considerable distress and weakening of the economic position of the people of the country anxious to secure independence from their government.
In connection with communist China, this means we are not opposed to selling wheat to communist China as such. The opposition we have shown to this sale, which we made plain in the election campaign and stand by at this time, is that this grain did not go to feed the hungry people of China. It was unscrupulously used by the communist government of that country for export to countries such as East Germany and Albania where the government of communist China was endeavouring to obtain political influence. We cannot believe that a country such as our own, believing in freedom, has the right to profit from trade that helps the cause of tyranny in this manner.
We also feel that, partly for humanitarian reasons and partly for strategic purposes in the cold war, Canadian exports of foodstuffs and other raw materials should primarily be directed to countries not under communist control, and only when the needs of these countries have been reasonably satisfied should surpluses be exported to communist countries. We strongly believe it is possible to work out practical trade arrangements with countries not under communist rule that will be beneficial both to them and to us and not leave Canada open to the charge of supporting her enemies while allowing her friends to go hungry.
This is a reasonable approach and one which will bear thinking about. Let us take a practical example. There are 450 million people in India. These people have a calorie intake of approximately only 1800 calories a day. There are hundreds of thousands of people who starve to death there each year. I know I have seen them die from starvation, and one does not forget such things. If we were to ship to India a bushel of wheat per head per year-450 million bushels of wheat- what would it represent? It would be 60 pounds of wheat per person, or approximately a loaf of bread a week. That is all. This does not only apply to India. It applies also to Pakistan, where the calorie intake on an average is only 1,810 calories per person a day. What about the countries in Latin America? What about the threat to communism in our own hemisphere? Is it not possible to work out trade problems and

Supply-Agriculture
extend trade credit arrangements in a better way than we are doing now? This is a question which I believe the Minister of Agriculture and the government must consider.
I believe it is wrong for us to take an isolationist stand with regard to the organization of American states. Here again an integrated policy must come into play. If we were playing our part in the organization of American states, which we all agree has greater economic potential than NATO has, we could go ahead and meet our needs as well as-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.
On behalf of this party I should like to give the leader of the Social Credit party the opportunity to finish his statement.
And I, on behalf of this party.

Thank you. In making this statement I am not trying to be destructive; I am not trying to spend hours of our time seeking to juggle the past record or confuse the issue which is before us now in the light of the past record. We are seeking to make a constructive contribution to the problem of trade as it relates to our agricultural industry.
I would say this also; that in meeting the problem of trading agreements which will provide for the distribution of our agricultural surpluses the time has come, imperatively so, when we should endeavour somehow to create an effective international settlements organization. I realize this is not the responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture, but it is the responsibility of the government.
Such action is necessary because the real difficulty in selling our agricultural products involves the settlement of obligations and the question of international trade agreements on a world scale. Until we can solve this problem of international settlements we shall be obliged to follow the very strategy which the other side in the cold war is seeking to force on us.
The world bank and the Bretton Woods agreement are failing to supply an effective system to facilitate world trade today. In 1945 the members of our group in this house took a strong stand on this and similar questions for reasons which we now see, in the light of subsequent events, to have been thoroughly justified. This is why I am confident we must move ahead in an effort to resolve this question of international payments in a long range manner rather than in

accordance with the expediencies of the hour. It is our responsibility, in this house of minorities, to do so; and the responsibility, specifically, of the government of the day.

Would the hon.
member permit a question? He is now on the subject of the financing and marketing of agricultural products. I wonder if he would tell the committee whether he is in favour of deficit financing.

The hon. member for
Acadia does not understand the requirements which enter the financial picture if we are to be able to solve this problem. If he is speaking of deficit financing as we think of it now, I say that deficit financing is the only answer. But is there any reason why a financial system which was thought out by our forefathers to meet the needs of their day should not be changed in order to meet the needs of our day? If we had a war we would settle it in a hurry.
Debt free money.

Yes, the hon. member
across the way is right. It does mean debt free money for the use of a two price system.
I hope the hon. member will not take exception to my remark. I was trying to call for applause for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
I also have a question-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has received permission to complete his remarks, and I think it would be better if further questions were not put to him.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I do not intend now to discuss in any detail how we recommend that the problem of international settlement should be met. Time does not permit, and there will be other opportunities to discuss it. I would say this, however; that if there was a hot war tomorrow we could export, without any selling price at all, billions upon billions worth of arms and never expect to be paid for them. Why can't we do that in time of peace? The committee may remember that when the last war was over we cancelled a billion dollars worth of debt owed by Great Britain, most of it on account of food supplied during the war, and nobody batted an eyelash about it. The need is just as urgent today.
I should like to say one thing more with regard to markets. The greatest market we have for our agricultural products is the Canadian market itself. As we consider the question of the international sale of our agricultural surpluses, let us make sure that we meet the needs of our own people as

well. It is time we made sure that our home market was satisfied, and I am thinking of areas of eastern Canada which were not blessed with the grain harvest they had in the west this year. They need it and should be able to take advantage of it as well.
It is time to make sure that our emergency measures organization includes stockpiles of food for every centre of the population should the catastrophe of war occur, and we all hope it will not.
However, we must not forget the need for the adequate trading agreements. The only way in which the world can go forward in the development of its resources, both material and human, is on the basis of the freest possible exchange of goods. That must mean a lowering, and in many cases the elimination, of various trade barriers. Again time does not permit to go into the details of this, but herein lies the approach we must take, and in this approach lies the solution to our problems. Canada and Canadians are waiting for leadership from this house which will work out a satisfactory solution to these problems before we are engrossed in a struggle with the direct threat of the take-over and the other side of this ideological war about which we have been talking.
So in closing-and I do appreciate the consideration of the members of this committee in letting me have a little extra time-I would say that it is all right to stand up and criticize the Minister of Agriculture, or to try to lay the blame at somebody else's doorstep. The fact remains that we ourselves will have to work out the solution. We in this corner of the house pledge our full co-operation in doing so. Only if we do this collectively can we face up to our responsibilities today in a world situation which, on the one hand, offers the greatest opportunity for development that civilization has ever known but, on the other hand, threatens us with the greatest period of dark ages that we can think of or which has ever been experienced. So let us, as we go on into this question, consider it constructively, not destructively, in order that we can fulfil our responsibilities.

Would the hon. member for Red Deer permit me under the rules to take exception to what I think was an inadvertent misstatement of fact? He said that the hon. member for Assiniboia was away from the house at the request or at the instance of the leader of the Liberal party. I may say that the hon. member for Assiniboia left this house yesterday with the assurance that an entirely different order of business was going to be up for consideration today. I am not
Supply-Agriculture
accusing anyone of having changed the order of business because the hon. gentleman was away, but that is the fact.

Mr. Chairman, may I say to the hon. gentleman for Bonavista-Twillingate that he should not put words into my mouth, because that is not what I said and it will not be found on the record. I merely noted that the hon. member for Assiniboia was absent today, and I did not attribute the reason for his absence to the leader of his party at all. The record will show that.
Well, I will leave it to Hansard.

Mr. Chairman, I will not get into the dispute between the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the leader of the Social Credit party regarding the absence of the hon. member for Assiniboia. It is probably quite within the usual procedure to have the leader of the Liberal party deal with agricultural matters on behalf of his party, and I am sure that the hon. member for Assiniboia is not here for reasons best known to himself. He has always been very considerate of his political leaders.
Because of the limited time at my disposal I propose to confine myself to discussing the question of wheat marketing and the statements which were made by the Minister of Agriculture when he addressed the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool on November 9. I would hope that at some later stage of our discussion of the agriculture estimates I might be able to discuss the wider field of agriculture and some of the questions of trade which have been raised this morning.
In opening the discussion of these estimates the other day, and in defending the statements which he made to the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the Minister of Agriculture did me the great honour of saying that my criticism of his statements demonstrated that I did not know anything about the operations of the wheat board. This may be true. I do not claim omniscience, as do some gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches, but I do want to say to the Minister of Agriculture that I was fighting in this house for the wheat board and for an orderly marketing system when the Minister of Agriculture was not quite sure as to the difference between May wheat and Mae West.
That is absolutely false in every detail.

I took exception, in the first place, to the fact that the minister should make what I consider to be two important statements on public policy before a meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool before any

Supply-Agriculture
statement had been made in this house or any opportunity given to any hon. members of this house to discuss it. I think any consideration which is so important that it affects the orderly marketing of wheat ought to be debated by the members of this house before a proposal is put forward which can only have the effect, as it has, of disturbing a great many farmers and, as I shall show, of disturbing the leaders of the various farm organizations.
The minister kept referring to the sentence in his speech which said:
I want to put forward a series of proposals which are in my mind-
The Prime Minister, in discussing this matter, also kept reiterating the phrase "which are in my mind". But I go on to finish the sentence:
-in the hope that there will be public discussion during the winter on these matters.
Surely a statement which is to have public discussion and a text which was distributed by the minister's own department could not be something which was merely in his mind. The minister defends himself on the ground that this was consultation with the farmers. No one objects to consultation with farm groups, but I do want to ask, first of all, why not begin by discussing this matter with the advisory committee of the wheat board?
One o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, before you leave the chair I wonder if I might suggest that there be unanimous agreement that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam be given the same latitude that was given to the hon. member for Red Deer. I believe the Minister of Agriculture intended that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It has already been done.
