At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

During the luncheon recess some of the members asked what was the difference between May wheat and Mae West. I am told on very good authority that the only way in which to find out is to accept the famous invitation "Come up and see me some time".

When we adjourned for luncheon I was dealing with the propriety of the minister making before the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool two extremely important proposals which had not been discussed in parliament. In defending his action he asked if I did not believe in consultation. Of course, anyone who has had anything to do with government knows that consultation is the very essence of good legislation. Certainly consultation with the advisory committee of the wheat board should have been done and perhaps was done. I hope the minister will tell us. Consultation with the executives of the various farm and wheat pool organizations would have been advisable.
However, the statements made by the minister were not in that category. It was not, as the Prime Minister suggested the other day, just a small meeting of farmers. This was the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool before which annually provincial and federal ministers have come to announce policy decisions. Far from being a private meeting, copies of this speech were distributed to the press. I would suggest that a statement of that kind becomes a statement of policy by the government. If it is not, then it is extremely difficult for farmers and for farm organizations to know when the Minister of Agriculture is speaking in his private capacity and when he is speaking in his official capacity.
On the surface the two proposals made by the Minister of Agriculture may seem to be fairly innocuous and even reasonable. However, they have implications which I think ought to be carefully examined. The farm organizations have spent the last 40 years battling to establish an orderly system of marketing wheat and coarse grains. This has been a long and difficult battle; the story of orderly marketing has a checkered career. The first wheat board was set up during the first world war. It was set up, I would remind the committee, not to keep prices up but rather to keep prices down. When the war was over the marketing of wheat was restored to the private grain trade and to the grain exchange with very disastrous results. The producers tried to protect themselves in the late 1920's by setting up their own central selling agency but without government backing this agency met some very serious reverses.
In the 1930's the demand for orderly marketing and for a wheat board to market grain became extremely vocal. Credit goes to the Conservative government under Right Hon. R. B. Bennett for setting up the wheat board in 1935, just as they were going out of office. It will be remembered that the first thing which the Liberal government did when they

came into office was to pass an order in council saying that wheat would not be handled by the wheat board as long as the price stayed above 90 cents a bushel. From this time until the beginning of the war wheat was handled mainly through the private grain trade. Again during the second world war the wheat board was made operative for the purpose of keeping the price down, not for the purpose of keeping it up. After the war public opinion in agricultural communities and indeed in all of western Canada was so clearly in favour of having orderly marketing and a national wheat board that it was impossible for any government to go back to handling wheat through the grain exchange. Hence we have had the wheat board ever since then.
The farmers have fought long and hard in order to get this type of orderly marketing and they have benefited from it. I take nothing away from the present Minister of Agriculture or the present government in saying that credit sales and increased sales have helped the farmers and that because of orderly marketing there have come to the farmers final payments which otherwise would have gone to the speculators. This is not just to the credit of the government. It is to the credit of all who through the years have fought for the establishment of an orderly system of marketing.
Now that we have such a system I suggest that we would do well to examine these two proposals of the minister with a view to seeing what their effect would be upon the scope and function of the Canadian wheat board as it is at present constituted. The first proposal made by the minister was that a final wheat payment could be used to build up a fund to share in any losses suffered through default on wheat credit sales abroad. I think perhaps I had better quote directly from the text of the minister's speech in which, at page 6, we find the following:
Specifically, I wish your organization at all levels to consider and discuss in a fully objective manner the possibility of "setting aside" a portion of the final wheat payment with a view to building up a fund which would be used in sharing in any loss which may occur, should there be a non-payment or default from a customer purchasing on a credit basis.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I want to ask this question. Why has this matter been raised at this particular time? No indication has come from any quarter to indicate that those nations which have been purchasing wheat on the credit basis are delinquent or are immediately likely to become delinquent. Why then are the farmers being asked to share any risk which may be involved? The minister
Supply-Agriculture
himself gave the reasons and I think they should be noted. He said, as found on page 6 of his address:
It was not an easy or simple matter to attain approval for these credit levels and I must advise you that it will become infinitely more difficult to obtain approval for higher levels, particularly when members of two opposition parties oppose these sales.
The minister did not say which parties they were and I leave it to him to corroborate his statement. Certainly this party is not one of them. But I ask, Mr. Chairman, was this a suggestion by the minister? Certainly it was not a suggestion. It was a clearcut statement that the minister did not find it easy to get his colleagues to agree to guarantees for these credit sales and that he would find it infinitely more difficult to get any further guarantees for credit sales. It is clear, therefore, that the reason this proposal was being put forth by the Minister of Agriculture was the reluctance on the part of his own colleagues to assume further responsibilities for large credits to enable the sale of wheat to overseas customers who are unable to pay cash. As a matter of fact, in the same paragraph the minister went on to say:
-it will make my task so much easier if I am able to say to my colleagues that farmers are willing to consider sharing the risk of credit sales.
I want to point out that this is a far cry from the speeches that were being made by the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues on the prairies during the last federal election campaign when they were saying to the farmers: The wheat board sold the wheat but we put up the money. It is a far cry from their speeches in which they were saying to the farmers: The government has guaranteed these credit sales and you will get your money. If these creditor nations fail to pay it will be the government that will take the loss. The farmers will not lose a cent.
But now we have a totally different story. Now we are being told that the cabinet are reluctant and, as the minister said, it will be infinitely more difficult to get them to underwrite further credit sales. I want to ask the question: Why should the cabinet hesitate about extending the level of credits for the sale of wheat? Guarantees to date amount to $190 million. Why should we consider that the ceiling? This is a comparatively small amount, as I shall show in a few moments, compared with what other countries which are exporters of wheat are doing.
It is true, as the minister pointed out, that under the Export Credits Insurance Act private exporters have guarantees of 85 per cent and they must carry 15 per cent of the risk themselves; but I would point out that

Supply-Agriculture
this is on the basis of sales which they themselves have negotiated. I think that the farmer is quite justified in saying that when the government has negotiated the sale and when the government, which is in a position to know, decides that this is a reasonably good risk, the government should be prepared to carry the risk. Certainly that view is shared by the farm leaders. I would point to the statement which was made by Mr. Rudy Usick, president of the Manitoba farmers union, who said:
Mr. Hamilton has promised to sell all the wheat the farmers could produce and it is not up to the farmers to bail him out when he gets in trouble.
Mr. W. J. Parker, president of the Manitoba pool elevators, said:
The farmers should not be asked to assume losses incurred by government policies.
I know of no reason why the government, on behalf of the agricultural population of western Canada, should not be prepared to assume any risks which may be involved. It seems to me that the government has a strange sense of priorities when it comes to dealing with the farmers. They have talked for years about a food bank. Yet I understand that Canada's contribution to the $100 million food bank is going to be a mere $5 million. Under the austerity program, which we are told does not exist, some $8 million has been cut from the paltry contribution we make under the Colombo plan. Now the government apparently is going to ask the farmers to underwrite the risk on credit sales, although no losses have been reported and so far we are told that no losses are anticipated.
What are you worried about?

One member asks me what I am worried about. I will tell him what I am worried about. I am worried about the farmers being asked to underwrite risks over which they have no control and being asked to underwrite the guesses of somebody else. That is what I am worried about.
Each year the government spends about $1,700 million on defence, and while I do not agree with the leader of the Social Credit party, who seemed this morning to have adopted Haushoffer's idea that food should become one of the weapons of war and that you starve people into submission-
Who said that?

That was the impression I certainly got from the hon. member. I do agree, however, that food is one of the weapons in the arsenal of democracy by which we can win for ourselves and for the cause in which we believe a great deal of

good will. We would do well to spend more money helping to feed the underprivileged and underdeveloped peoples of the world. This in the long run would do more to contribute toward peace than probably any other single thing we could do.
I would point out that the United States has gone much further than Canada has in promoting wheat sales abroad by means of government aid. This morning the Leader of the Opposition said that we had to question whether or not too much of the sale of our wheat was being carried out on the basis of credit sales as related to cash sales. Everybody knows that we would always prefer to make sales for cash but I should like to point out that in the 1960-61 crop year United States exports of wheat and flour totalled 660 million bushels and that almost 70 per cent of that was disposed of by other than cash terms. In contrast, Canada's credit sales represented a relatively small fraction of our total sales. Both the Australian and French governments have concluded major agreements to sell wheat to China on much more favourable terms than those allowed by Canada. This suggests that the Canadian government has not even come close to reaching the maximum level of guarantees for export credits which it could properly make in respect of wheat sales abroad.
What are you worrying about the risk for?

The hon. member seems to want to keep interrupting. I suggest he will have an excellent opportunity to stand up before this debate is concluded and tell this committee and the farmers of western Canada whether or not he favours the proposal of the Minister of Agriculture.
I certainly do, and I am going to go back and tell them so.
Perhaps the hon. member will repudiate it like the Prime Minister did.
I thought I made myself quite clear in saying I will support them and will take part in the debate.
You will support both sides.

The hon. member will support one here and another one in the country.
What is disturbing to those of us who believe in and have fought for an orderly marketing system is that this could be the camel's nose in the tent. This could be the beginning of something that will go much further. In the minister's speech to the wheat pool delegates, he said, "I have no exact share in mind." We have a right to know what share the minister has in mind. Are the

farmers, bit by bit, going to be saddled with more and more of the insurance risk? Is the responsibility for underwriting overseas wheat credits gradually going to be shifted from the government to the farmers? This is what we want to know. If we are going to sell wheat, then credit sales are going to become an increasingly important factor. I am told, and the minister can tell us more as the committee proceeds, that under the agreement with communist China the latter has now taken sufficient wheat to have passed the minimum and she does not have to take any more. She can take more, but is not required to do so. This may mean negotiations for any further wheat sales. As I have already mentioned France, Australia and the United States are already offering very favourable terms. If credit sales are going to be an increasingly important factor in the sale of wheat to overseas customers, then the farmers are justified in wanting to know whether this is only the thin end of the wedge; whether or not step by step the whole burden is going to be passed over to them.
The second proposal made by the minister is contained on page 7 of his manuscript. I quote:
I am now going to put forward a second major suggestion for serious consideration and discussion. Will the three western pools, and the United Grain Growers, acting co-operatively, consider forming a grain sales organization to enter aggressively, first the domestic market and secondly, at a later stage, the export market as a real selling agent of the Canadian wheat board?
I would say that this proposal implies that the wheat board has not been doing an effective job in selling wheat and that an additional agency might be helpful. My own opinion is that the Canadian wheat board has been doing an admirable job and has functioned quite well as a selling agency. If the minister feels that the farm organizations could make a contribution, then of course he could give them greater representation by adding their representatives to the wheat board. The pool organizations already have export departments. These, of course, could be enlarged. But when the minister says the farmers want to be independent, I should like to tell him they want to be independent but they do not want to be deserted. They do not want to have this responsibility transferred from the wheat board to the farmers.
We should never lose sight of the fact that nearly the entire world wheat trade today is now conducted on the basis of what might be called state trading. Under present day conditions, governments mainly deal with governments. For those customers who are not able to pay, insurance arrangements have been worked out between the various nations to
Supply-Agriculture
sell for credit, in some cases to accept foreign exchange and in other cases by straight barter exchange. In such a situation I believe that only the government can effectively handle the overseas selling of wheat. The experience of the central selling agency in the thirties showed the limitation of a producer group if it lacked government backing in being able to operate successfully. It would be worse than useless to expect that any producer selling agency to be able to compete abroad for wheat sales with the national treasury of the United States, France or Australia.
I said the other day, in my opinion, these proposals represent a devious undermining of the scope, functions and responsibilities of the wheat board as presently constituted. The minister said that this statement was entirely false. Well, I point out that the leaders of the three farm unions of Canada, Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, have expressed concern and opposition; that the secretary manager of the Manitoba Federation of Agriculture has said the same thing, and that the president of the Manitoba pool has expressed disagreement.
Why are these people concerned? They are concerned because these two proposals do not seem to be completely unrelated. The wheat board has told us, through their annual report, that more and more of their sales are being handled by their agents and less directly by the wheat board itself. I was rather interested in noticing the other day that the minister said the wheat board is not mainly responsible for selling. Well, this was not the story that government members were telling on the hustings last May and June. They were saying, we have sold wheat; we have put up guarantees. Now, they are saying, we want you to start taking the risks; we want you to start assuming the responsibility for selling.
That is nonsense.

The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek thinks it is nonsense. He has a chance to tell the people what he thinks. He can take part in this debate, but he will probably keep out of it; I know what his job has been. It has been simply to vote the way he is told and keep quiet the rest of the time.
If the wheat board is going to divest itself in increasing measure of responsibility for selling, and if the government is going to divest itself increasingly of responsibility for guaranteeing credit sales, what will be the result? The result will be that a producers organization, unless it has the support of the Canadian treasury, will find itself carrying major risks and this could be the beginning of

Supply-Agriculture
a return to the private grain trade and to the old grain exchange speculative market. Let us make no mistake about that. Mr. Chairman, I say that I am suspicious of these two proposals.
Too suspicious.

Someone says, "Too suspicious". I would like to tell hon. members sitting on the government side that I have good reason to be suspicious. When I see what this government has done to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which they have undermined in the interests of the private broadcasting network; when I see what they have done to the T.C.A., which they sabotaged in the interests of Canadian Pacific Airlines; when I see what they have been doing to the Canadian National Railways-
Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Keep in order.
-where it has transpired in the last few days that when a potash mine is opened in Saskatchewan and the Canadian National Railways is quite capable-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but we are on the first item of agriculture, which allows a very broad scope on that subject but not on other subjects.

Mr. Chairman, with all deference I suggest that I am simply illustrating that a government which could sabotage the C.B.C., T.C.A. and the C.N.R. is equally capable of sabotaging the Canadian wheat board. I am saying that when Canadian National Railways was quite able to handle all the potash, had the cars, had the arrangements made, Conservative members supported the C.P.R. in building a parallel line which was constructed before they even came to this parliament, and they did this by giving their support to the passage of a private bill to give the railway authority to construct a line.
Did you vote against it?

I certainly did vote against it; I opposed it in this house. I opposed that bill on second reading, as anyone who looks at the record will know. Also, I would point out that when the bill was before the committee our members took very serious exception to duplicating this line and said there was no reason why Canadian National Railways should not have been given an opportunity to demonstrate whether or not it could handle this traffic. The petitioners were so anxious that they had the line started before they even brought the legislation into the house.

This is why farm leaders in western Canada are apprehensive of the proposals put before them by the minister; not just because of the two proposals in themselves, but because they have dangerous undertones and dangerous implications for the continued operation of the wheat board and for the maintenance of an orderly marketing system in the handling of wheat. As a matter of fact, the very first step toward undermining the wheat board was taken by this government last year when they took feed grains out from under the wheat board and returned these to the private trade.
You had better stick to medical care.

Mr. Chairman, I will tell my hon. friend who made that interjection that any Tory party representative who goes out through western Canada and tries to sell these two proposals to the prairie farmer will need psychiatric care, never mind medical care. I am suggesting that the time has come, not for the government to give less support to the processes of orderly marketing but to give more support.
The wheat situation is not as rosy as government supporters have been trying to tell the public over the last year. The recent report shows that wheat stocks, by the government's own statement, now amount to about 953 million bushels. This, if I remember correctly, is about the third highest in our record. The estimate is that they will sell, between export and consumption in Canada, some 470 million bushels; that amount will be disposed of in this crop year. This will leave us by July 31, 1963 with about 480 million bushels. If we have a better than average crop next summer, this means we will have a larger carryover next year than we have at the present time.
With the levies that are being imposed by the European common market, added to the fact that the United States today has about two billion bushels of wheat in stock, that Europe has good crops and that both France and Australia are pushing into the world export market by extending very favourable credit terms, this means that Canada is going to have to sell wheat on the basis of state trading. It is going to have to underwrite more, and not less, sales. This is a responsibility which belongs to the government and the government cannot divest itself of that responsibility. For the government to endeavour to throw back upon the wheat producers responsibilities which are properly those of the government is something which

I believe will be resisted by the wheat growers of western Canada, and I can assure the government it will be resisted by the members of this party.

Mr. Chairman, first of all let me say that I am sorry you could not hear all the remarks that were passed at this end of the chamber. I think that possibly, if they all appeared on the record, it would be one of the funniest periods in this house since I have been here. I laughed when I heard the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam speak about Mae West. He is an expert on this type of subject. But I come from Saskatchewan and I have heard him say the same thing for 30 years. To me it is the same old, well worn gramophone record that he plays every time he gets up to speak. This gramophone record is getting pretty monotonous in Saskatchewan.
I know at least two good reasons why his statement is wrong. One is this: while he was preaching in another arena I was attending meetings of western Conservatives in the early 1930's that eventually led not only to the formation of the Canadian wheat board in 1935, but also in no small measure to the farm loan act amendments, the farmers' credit re-arrangement act amendments, the Natural Products Marketing Act and a whole series of legislation aimed at helping farmers all across this country. He came into the picture in 1935 at the time when Mae West was at her peak. Now he gets up in the house and says it was improper for me to consult with my own constituents before I consult with hon. members here in Ottawa. I suppose he defines my constituents as being delegates of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. He says it is not right for me to consult with them first. I suggest to him that if he had consulted with the people of Saskatchewan before he tried to ram that medicare scheme on them, he would not have had to leave Saskatchewan.
Then the hon. gentleman goes on to raise the bogeyman that this government which, after years of tribulation, established the Canadian wheat board and is now trying to tear it down. I am not going to deal point by point with everything the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has said, because he demonstrated again in this house today that he knows so much less about the marketing of grain than the majority of our Conservative backbenchers that I shall leave him to take his chance with them. For example, he said he thought this government should do more. Does he not remember that the first thing the government did this session was to 27507-3-124
Supply-Agriculture
double the funds available to back the Export Credits Insurance Act, from $200 million to $400 million?

What has that got to do with
it?

There you have a perfect example of the knowledge of the New Democratic party. Under section 21 of the Export Credits Insurance Act, some $170 million are committed today. Of that sum, approximately $90 million is for wheat. That is what it has to do with it.
Could I ask the minister why the other $100 million did not come under the same section?

The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is a glutton for punishment. That is exactly what I was trying to do in western Canada two weeks ago-call attention to the fact that new opportunities exist, opportunities about which the hon. member apparently knows nothing and cares nothing. All he is interested in doing, to judge from his remarks today, is to make sure that the farmers of western Canada have no chance of forming a selling agency so that those who produce the wheat should have a chance to get some of the profits on its sale.
They have that right now.

They , have that right now. After a lifetime of regaling us, in Saskatchewan in particular, about the evil of monopoly interests and the threat of these giant corporations which have so much say in controlling the movement of goods in world markets, the hon. member now says we must not let farmers form a sales organization to get into this field because it is one which should be reserved for those friends of his, the great international grain companies. That is what, in effect, he is saying-though he does not know what he is saying; that is the kindest thing one can say of him.
But I did not rise to castigate the physical giant from Burnaby-Coquitlam. I will let him take his chance with the backbenchers. My remarks on this occasion will be on other subjects. It is not usual for a minister bringing down his estimates, particularly an earthy, simple type like the Minister of Agriculture, to have such attention paid to him by the leaders of three parties. I could not altogether understand why the leader of the Liberal party should have got into this. I thought perhaps he was sensitive about the fact that when he made that long oration of his during the debate on the address he omitted to say anything at all about agriculture, and had to make up for it somehow. Then it

Supply-Agriculture
occurred to me that the second reason why he wished to speak on this subject was because someone had advised him-I do not know who-that it might be wise for him to attack the Minister of Agriculture so that all the credit would not go to the party called the New Democratic party. I do not know who advised the hon. gentleman. I know that in the days when the hon. member for Essex East advised him he had a good adviser. Although that hon. member knew nothing about agriculture, he had his own bureau of statistics and any advice he gave to the Leader of the Opposition at least did not get the hon. gentleman into trouble. But the hon. member for Algoma East now has a new adviser, and this adviser has a remarkable record of being wrong. Whenever an issue comes up in agriculture, 90 per cent of the time the hon. member for Assiniboia goes the wrong way, and any person who observes someone going the wrong way over and over again generally goes the other way as a matter of common sense, if he has any judgment.
When I made those remarks in Regina, the hon. member for Assiniboia rushed immediately into print and, in phrases which usually can be found only in the Leader-Post gave vent to such expressions as "preposterous, incredible, fantastic." No, he did not say "peanuts" that time. It brought to my mind the time we sold the wheat to China. He was out west at that point fighting to be leader of the New Democratic party. He rushed back here and said: "The China deal is a myth; it is a pipe dream; it is a hoax; it does not exist; it is nothing." But when the farmers got their cheques last April they knew what "nothing" really was. Here we find the hon. member coming out once again and saying: This is fantastic, preposterous, incredible. Not to be outdone, the leader of the New Democratic party rushes into the house on Monday and moves the adjournment in order to discuss the very ordinary speech I made asking the farmers to consider matters which primarily concerned them alone.
Then we had this report to the Leader of the Opposition. But why did the Leader of the Opposition zig when he should have zagged? Whenever you see the hon. member for Assiniboia going one way, then, if you are smart, you should go the other way. This zigging and zagging business is something which the Leader of the Opposition should learn and remember. I do not really blame a man the first time he makes a mistake, but I cannot understand the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam not knowing that he should zig when the other is zagging, because he has surely learned from his long

experience that when the hon. member for Assiniboia zigs he should certainly zag, if he is not to be entirely wrong.
However, the Leader of the Opposition has only made his first mistake. On the first two occasions when I heard the hon. member for Assiniboia speak in this house during the present session I was careful to ask whether he was speaking for the Liberal party. The first time I did so the answer came reluctantly; the second time, the hon. member was a little more confident. I can only surmise at this time that he must have been first at his leader's ear with his advice. He led his leader into a trap, because at the very moment his leader was standing up in this house and saying that my two proposals made to a farm organization were ridiculous, the farmers, after five days of cogitating about this matter in solemn convention-and these wheat pool delegates are not panicked by spokesmen for certain political parties; they look at a question and study it; they do not take these things haphazardly-at the very moment the Leader of the Opposition was denying me the right to finish my statement in the house on Wednesday, November 14, the farmers of Saskatchewan, through their wheat pool delegates, were voting in favour of two resolutions which were moved in order to accomplish what I asked them to do, namely to study these two proposals.

Mr. Chairman, I am rising on a question of privilege, because I was the person who offered, on behalf of this party, to give the Minister of Agriculture unlimited time to speak that day, if the government was willing to carry on the debate consecutively, as should have been done; and it was the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre who denied the minister the right to go. The record in Hansard shows that.
May I ask the minister to read those two resolutions which have been referred to?
I think the sensitivity of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate shows that his hide may be as thick as a rhinoceros, but you cannot get underneath it.
I just believe in telling the truth.
Mr. Chairman, I was saying-
The minister referred to two resolutions passed by the annual meeting of the wheat pool. Would he like to read those resolutions?
You had your speech.
If the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam will compose himself-
I think the committee should have them on the record.
Like him, I want to make my speech. I was pointing out that at the time, through whatever technique he used, the Leader of the Opposition was refusing me the right-
That is another falsehood.
When the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said that he would give the minister five minutes on condition-
Not at all.
-to give the house leader time to get the program for the next day from the Minister of Finance-
Read what is on Hansard.

I want to get on to my main point-at that very moment when the Leader of the Opposition was rising to his feet-I will put it that way-and I was not allowed to finish my statement, he was not aware of it at the time, but he was pulling the skewers on to his own chest and impaling himself on those skewers. Because next morning when wires were humming all across the country that the western farmers, through the Saskatchewan wheat pool, were supporting me, where did that leave the Leader of the Opposition? Because he had already said that my two statements were ridiculous. As a matter of fact, the next day the headline on the front page of the Winnipeg Free Press said: "Pearson blasts Hamilton's speech". That headline was written by Victor Mackie, and right underneath it appeared the words: "Pool backs Hamilton".
That is more than the Prime Minister did.

I suggest to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that his sensitivity indicates to me that I have scored again. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asks for these resolutions. This is the news despatch of November 15. One resolution said:
The Saskatchewan wheat pool, in co-operation with the Alberta and Manitoba pools, should investigate methods of setting up a joint fund to underwrite the risk assumed by the federal government in granting credit to communist countries for the purchase of grain.
The second resolution recommended:
-that the Saskatchewan wheat pool investigate the possibility of setting up a joint export department with the Alberta and Manitoba pools to promote sales abroad of Canadian grain.

All I ask is that the hon. member study those resolutions; I am not asking for anything more at the present time.
If hon. members would like to hear just what was going on, I should like to put my thoughts forward to them, so that instead of setting up bogeymen and talking about something, I say in all kindness, they know not too much about, if they had a few more facts maybe their criticisms would be a shade more on target. These points of view are debatable.
Would the minister permit a question?
Certainly.

In putting these views forward, is the minister speaking for the government as Minister of Agriculture, or is he just putting his own personal views forward? I think the committee is entitled to know that.
Whenever my colleagues decide that I am not Minister of Agriculture they will tell me, not the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Apparently the Prime Minister said you were not the other day.

On Wednesday, November 14, I was speaking about the way the wheat board operates. I read into the record two quotations from a pamphlet produced by one of the distinguished commissioners of the Canadian wheat board. This pamphlet pointed out that the board gathered its grain from agents, who are competing one against the other in the gathering of this grain. I then pointed out in the second section that the board then distributed this grain to other agents who were licensed under the board to sell this grain around the world. Now, approximately 40 agents have these licences. As a matter of record, I believe the pools have these licences but do not use them. It is true that one of the pools sells some flour, but generally speaking these 40 agents of the Canadian wheat board who sell the grain the wheat board collects are private agencies, and by far the greater percentage of the grain sold by the Canadian wheat board to these agents is to the large international companies who have done a tremendously efficient job of selling our grain, as well as the grain of France, the United States, Argentina, and any other country with grain to sell. That is their business.
When I was giving the house some of these quotations from the pamphlet so as to try and stop opposition members making any more mistakes in their public statements, my 30 minutes came to an end. I was just at the

Supply-Agriculture
point where I was going to go on to point out that instead of, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam says, the whole world turning towards state trade, actually in this last ten years the reverse has been the case. Therefore I will now try and give the committee some tangible evidence to show just how this government has gone out and given some incentive-I should not say incentive, but has given some encouragement-to the wheat board to do that part of its operations which are done from government to government. Mr. Chairman, I would ask that this table be put on Hansard in its completeness, because it is valuable. These figures are for all the years I could conveniently get, and I think they are all the figures we have at the moment. In the year 1955 to 1956, for instance-
Could the minister say where the figures are from?

These are the Canadian wheat board figures extracted from their records, and I got them from the Canadian wheat board. The table should be called: "Table percentage of export of wheat and flour covered by master sales contracts, 19551962." Mr. Chairman, you will recall that in the last statement I made I pointed out that ordinarily the grain of the Canadian wheat board is turned over to private agencies for sale. But when it is a matter of government sales, then the wheat board comes in and does the negotiating and works out the agreements. In the year 1955-1956, which was the last full year that the previous government were in power, the quantities looked after by the Canadian wheat board, which in this table will appear as "quantity covered by master sales contracts," was 3.9 million bushels, and the quantity sold for cash, was 312 million bushels. This is one of the better years. The percentage figure showing what the wheat board sold, in relation to what the private trade sold under the Liberals, shows the figure of 1.27 per cent sold directly by the Canadian wheat board. I think that shows the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that if you go back over the previous years you will find that of this business perhaps 5 per cent would be the general average of what the wheat board sold.
I wonder if the minister would permit a question?
Yes, if it is on this subject.
My question is with reference to this table and just where we might find it. For what year is that report?

It is taken from the Canadian wheat board figures and is not found

in the annual report because it has never been asked for in this form. However, that is where I got them from, namely the Canadian wheat board. For the next year 1956-57, the percentage of grain sold under master sales contracts went up to 34.6 million bushels. This was the year of the Polish agreement. Because sales dropped so low on the cash side the total sales that year were approximately $264 million and the percentage of exports covered by master sales contracts that year was 9.32. In 1957-58, you might call these the Conservative years-the master contracts went up to $41.4 million that year and the total sale to $320 million. I give credit publicly as I have done many times to the Minister of Veterans Affairs who was then in charge of the Canadian wheat board. Then there was a much bigger sale to the extent of nearly 60 million bushels that year over the previous year but the percentage of total exports covered by master sales contracts had risen to 12.9 or nearly 13 per cent. In 1958-59- and I will just give the percentages now because I want to get on with my remarks- the percentage was 10.52; in 1959-60 it was 11.6; in 1960-61 it was 19.9; and in 1961-62- that is the last crop year-it was 27.99 per cent. An increase from 1 per cent to 27 per cent in seven years shows who has been giving the encouragement to the Canadian wheat board to sell.
Mr. Chairman, I have another question I wish to ask the minister.
I would ask permission to have this table printed in Hansard at this point as part of my speech.

Consent has been given.
Consent has not been given.

I have been on my feet trying to get the chairman's attention. I should like to have the minister's assurance if he will give it to the committee that these figures are verifiable from the wheat board record. I am puzzled by the manner of delivery. Second, I should like to have his assurance that those sales were actually not made through the wheat board, because these are very puzzling percentages. I should like his assurance that these figures can be verified in the wheat board reports.
I am glad to give the hon. member that assurance. I said these figures came from the Canadian wheat board and they take full responsibility for them.

I thank the minister. He may have the consent which he requested.

May I ask the minister a question?
Yes.
How does this prove the contrary of my statement that we are moving more and more to state trading? Does it not support and corroborate what I said?
Yes, it does, since we came into the operations these last four or five years; but generally speaking over the world what I say is still true.
Not in the United States, where 70 per cent of their export wheat was sold for other than cash.

Yes, it would be to the Far East. But if you take the world market for grain today as given in your report, then I think the percentage sold on the commercial market is in the main rising steadily, and this is mainly because of expansion of the private trading concerns. I could give a good example of that in the sales of French wheat this last few months through the private sector of the economy, which will increase this instead of decrease it.
I left off where I was trying to make it clear that generally speaking since this government came into power we have given this encouragement to the wheat board that has increased a number of master sales agreements. In all fairness I would point out that in this selling operation not only is the greater
Supply-Agriculture
bulk sold by the very efficient private trade, but there is an increasing percentage, because of credit sales negotiated by the Canadian wheat board. However, the ministers of the crown talked to members of various governments of the world trying to sell wheat too. Members of the trade and commerce department who are in these various centres of the world are always on the alert looking for increased opportunities to sell.
I would say here at this time that in spite of all these little rumours and fears that are running around, in the next two or three years the future for Canadian sales on the export market, both in cash and in credit, are good. No matter how good it may be, I think it is my duty not to be complacent. I naturally ask myself today what else can be done. I tell this committee that I have spoken to some of the large international grain companies and have questioned them about some of the activities in order to see if it would not be possible for them to do more than they are doing. They are doing a good job. However, have I not a right as one responsible to parliament and to the people for the sale of Canadian grain, to ask our agents if they are doing all that it is possible to do and maybe suggest a few other ways where there is additional opportunity.
I do that. I have talked to the Canadian companies the same way. I have talked to them particularly about the markets in eastern Canada for domestic grain because I know the story of what is going on in the Ottawa valley and in the eastern part of this country, and what is behind it. I am not going to talk about the developments in West Germany. They are important now. It gives a good opportunity for them to carry out the function of trade in their countries. I have talked to the new ambassadors going to these new countries of Africa. They know where I stand. Most of them come to my office before they go on their tour of duty and find out how they can help best the combined effort. Private trade, the Canadian wheat board through its contacts and its officials, government officials in trade and commerce, and so on-even the diplomats in effect are taking off their striped pants and putting on their overalls in order to sell wheat.
I am not entirely satisfied with this. Here you have those of us in the selling-

speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture may continue.
Up to now, to whom do we sell wheat outside of Canada and the United States?

I think there are some-and I would not be sure of the exact number- I think we sell wheat to some 45 or 48 countries. We do sell on a cash basis in other countries both wheat and flour and also we sell at the present time on credit in China, Poland and Czechoslovakia.
What are the main ones?

The five main countries would be the United Kingdom, Japan, China, possibly West Germany next, and then Poland, I suppose. These are the big customers. We sell very little wheat to the United States -just seed wheat. I was trying to build a case here. I was trying to encourage every agency with respect to which we have some influence to sell even more. Here you have the government declaring its interest by doubling the amount of credit available under the Export Credits Insurance Act from $200 million to $400 million, thus providing greater leeway and opportunity in the making of sales. The government is willing to redouble its efforts.
I know the history of the western wheat pools. I know that they were originally formed to sell grain. I know that because of their unhappy experience in the late '20's- 1928 and 1929-they went broke and I know how they were saved by the provincial governments and the federal government making loans to them which they have paid back completely. But they have stayed out of the business of selling grain ever since. It has been left to the private grain trade to handle our grain ever since.
It is true that the Canadian wheat board gathers all the grain and turns it over to these other companies as their agents, for
[The Deputy Chairman.]
sale, but there is not a single Canadian company owned by producers of wheat in that list of agents. What I was doing was asking these hardheaded farmers of the Saskatchewan wheat pool simply to consider if there was not a possibility that they could restore the dream they had 40 years ago of producers not only making money out of the handling and storage of grain but also out of the marketing of grain. That is all that I was asking and that is why the members of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, one of the great co-operatives in western Canada, did not turn down my request to study the matter.
They knew 1 was asking them to go down to eastern Canada as a start and see if they could not help the government get western feed grain to the eastern farmers more cheaply by competing with others who are selling in that area. They know why I asked for their help. I told them that the farmers of eastern Canada needed their help; I asked for unity between east and west and I said to them that if the eastern farmers could not organize themselves for the purpose of purchasing feed grain, why could the western farmers not say: O.K., we will go down there and service our customers because they are our friends, our fellow Canadians and fellow producers. That is all I asked them. Could we have another agency of the board in addition to the 40 existing ones, just one more agency owned by the producers which would provide an additional Canadian incentive for increased sales?
I should like to quote at this time what I said at the pool meeting. It has been read into the record, but to keep my own remarks coherent I should like to read that section of my speech. First of all, may I say that in my opening remarks I spoke of all the new opportunities in new countries where we were not selling wheat today at all-not China, but countries like China which we could not bring under the Export Credits Insurance Act because of the lack of a credit rating. I described the opportunities in these new countries over the next 10 or 20 years and I said:
I am now going to put forward a second majoi suggestion for serious consideration and discussion. Will the three western pools and the United Grain Growers, acting co-operatively, consider forming a grain sales organization to enter aggressively first the domestic market and, second, at a later stage, the export market, as a real selling agent of the Canadian wheat board?
The use of the word "real" is obvious. They have a licence to sell but they do not use it. I asked them if they would form this selling agency and go into eastern Canada and see what they could do about bringing western grain into that area.

You will recall that this was the original purpose of the pools. Now in this period of intense international competition, new and unforeseen opportunities are being presented to us by ever-enlarging markets in newly developing countries.
No talk about China, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Russia, but rather of the newly developing countries.
I think this is a crucial moment in the history of the western pools and the United Grain Growers. I am completely aware of the tremendous competitive and complex nature of the grain business in the world. I am completely aware of the tremendous drive and efficiency of the great national and international grain companies and carriers. I recognize and appreciate their service and helpfulness as agents of the Canadian wheat board. But as a Canadian I put it to you that there Is a need for a great Canadian grain co-operative sales organization, particularly when you consider that so much of our domestic market in eastern Canada is serviced by co-operatives and particularly when you consider that many of our importing countries are state trading nations.
What do I get for making this suggestion? Nothing but criticism the like of which we have heard today.
And repudiation by the Prime Minister.
That is ridiculous.
The case of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is pretty weak when he keeps harping on that point.
Just cabinet solidarity; that is all.

You are the great expert who knows all about cabinet solidarity, the man who was described by a man now dead as a high placed leak.
I should like to refer to a statement of the type we have heard in the house again today. This appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of November 12, just before I came back to Ottawa. This statement is credited to the leader of the New Democratic party. The article is by a member of the Free Press staff located in Ottawa and quotes the leader of the New Democratic party as follows:
It is therefore important that in selling wheat abroad the sole responsibility for this function should remain with the Canadian wheat board.
"The sole responsibility for this function should remain with the Canadian wheat board". The sole responsibility, Mr. Chairman, never has rested with the Canadian wheat board and a man who makes that kind of statement exposes the depth of his knowledge of how the wheat board operates.
If the board's selling efficiency abroad can be improved by the adding of representatives from the co-operative grain marketing agencies then such representatives could quite easily be added to the present board without detracting from the responsibility which can only be handled effectively by a government marketing agency.
Sup p ly-A griculture
I do not blame the leader of the New Democratic party for going back to that old socialist philosophy which he discarded in Saskatchewan 20 years ago, now that he is in a new field with a new crop of suckers to harvest; but we in Saskatchewan have got used to that tune and know that in Saskatchewan he no longer talks about socialism, but that he is a man who believes in socialism cooperating with private enterprise, with private enterprise doing 90 per cent of the work. Now he goes back to the old gramophone record about state trading. This was a theory that was going to remove all our taxes in Saskatchewan but it did not work out in that way so he changed the tune. He has changed his tune again in the national field and I want to point out that this is not a man into whose hands one would want to put the responsibility of running this country.
May I ask the minister a question? Does the minister say that the wheat board as now constituted has not the sole responsibility for marketing wheat?
The wheat board has the sole responsibility for marketing wheat, but it turns it over at Fort William, Churchill and Vancouver to private trading companies and private trading companies only.
But the responsibility is still that of the wheat board.

Yes, they are just a handling agency. When I read these remarks I know that one person at least does not understand how the Canadian wheat board operates. As I also said earlier, this puts him in a position where I know he does not want to be. He is now in a position in western Canada where he says he does not want the producers to have their own company selling grain as the agent of the Canadian wheat board. This activity now must be reserved for these private trading companies. He does not want to be in this position, but that is where he is. This is the hole he is going to have to dig himself out of. This is exactly the hole the Leader of the Opposition, too, is going to have to dig himself out of. I cannot blame the hon. member for Assiniboia for being lucky all the time because he is absent today, but that is the hole he is in, too. It was for this reason the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate left, because he did not want to get too far into that hole.
I do not know whether the western pools will decide to set up a selling agency; that is their decision, not ours. They are going to have to put up the dollars; they are going to have to put up the know-how. They are going to have to take the risk of losing money as well as making it, because both

Supply-Agriculture
things happen when you go into the selling business. However, believe me, the Canadian wheat board is strengthened, not weakened every time a new organization enters the field of selling Canadian grain as one of their agents. I think if it is good to have 40 agents, it is better to have 41. The wheat board approves because that is what they say in their pamphlets.
Let me say, in so far as consultation is concerned, that I spoke to the Canadian wheat board at great length about this proposal and they said it would be a wonderful thing if we had a purely Canadian producer company joining in the competition of selling our products.
And the advisory committee?

And I spoke to those members concerned of the advisory committee. In fact, I spoke to them about a year ago. The mere fact that they came out and said, "We have been studying this for the last few months," indicates that what I say is true. I want the producers to have a say anyway in the handling of their grain. If they want to take the risks and get the opportunity of making money out of selling their grain, then they should have it. This is where I differ with the Leader of the Opposition and his adviser, the hon. member for Assiniboia and the leader of the New Democratic party. I want more people in the swim.
Now, I am not going to lengthen these remarks unduly. There is one point I should like to put on the record. The real issue here, Mr. Chairman, is not this speech. The real issue is not these two suggestions. The real issue is the fact that, over there in the Liberal opposition they know they can never be the government of this country until they destroy the confidence the farmers of this country have in the present government. This is the real issue. They have decided to put their faith in the remarks of some of these farm leaders. These same farm leaders came out for deficiency payments, and the farmers gave them their answer on June 18. These same farm leaders came out for sales to feed mills, and the farmers gave their answer on that.
These same people had doubt about a lot of the things this government has done. I intend to go to more meetings of these farm organizations that are mentioned here and put suggestions before them, too. I want to know what the rank and file of these organizations believe, not only their leaders. This is what I did in the fall of 1960, and hon. members should read the press reports in Winnipeg, Edmonton and Saskatoon when those speeches were made. I went there with ideas different
from those which the farm leaders were espousing, and I got the reception I did, not only after my speech but after the two hour question period that followed. I put my case before the people because I have learned to trust the people and not the politicians.
This is a matter of record. The Leader-Post of Regina is not known as a Conservative paper. Listen to what it says in the lead editorial of November 16, 1962. Those who sit in the seats of the official opposition should listen and learn because when the Leader-Post says these things they do not do so lightly. I quote:
The alacrity with which some of the politicians condemned agriculture minister Hamilton's proposals on grain marketing, and the extravagance of some of the adverse criticism, are astonishing.
Farther down the editorial states:
Mr. Hamilton's proposals are worthy of a better fate than precipitate condemnation by self-seeking politicians.
Who are these self-seeking politicians? Every one of them is absent, with one exception.

May I ask the minister a question? Is it not true that the Regina Leader-Post has always been against the wheat board, against orderly marketing, and always been the champion of the private grain trade?
Mr. Chairman, they have always been against the Conservatives, I know that.
No, they were not last June.

The hon. member does not read the same paper I read.
This is my final point. Since the issue is really the destruction of the faith of the farmer in the only government which, for years, has made a move in his direction, just as he is starting to find his place in the sun, they know they have to destroy this confidence. What is the target they are setting? They are setting their guns really on this China wheat sale. This is the target on which they have to zero in, because if they do not destroy these sales to mainland China they have no hope of ever gaining strength, not only in western Canada in the farm constituencies but across this great dominion from sea to sea.
They argue that we are the only country that continues trading with mainland China. They say that while Chinese guns are shooting down Indian soldiers, we are feeding the mainland Chinese people. Mr. Chairman, I want to conclude with the highlights of what I have been trying to say. As Minister of Agriculture I have the responsibility and duty to consult with those engaged in the farm industry of this country. This need for consultation is greater now than at any time in our history. I hope to continue that pattern of behaviour.
Second, never has the wheat board been stronger, both at the domestic level of its operations and in the field of foreign sales. However, I hold to the principle that no matter how good we may think things are, they might be better.

Supply-Agriculture
Third, I say that the China sale was good for Canada, and is good for Canada. I hope that world conditions will be such that in the years ahead all nations will find it possible to increase their normal commercial trade with China, and I feel that all men of good will would wish to see the humanitarian objective of providing food for hungry people be given an even higher priority than it is today, either by gifts, cash sales or credit sales.
My objectives and purposes in making my Regina speech were; first, to build up the Canadian wheat board and enlarge its sales operations; not to tear down or diminish the role of the board. Second, to enlarge the opportunities of western farmers and their co-operatives, both in expanding the markets for their products and in sharing in the profits of marketing as well as in the handling of grain; not to impose new obligations on western farmers. Third, to acknowledge the important role of the private trade in maintaining our high position in export markets and to urge a further intensification of their efforts; not to diminish the role or the opportunities of the private trade.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to address a question to the minister. I believe he said, about 20 minutes ago in his remarks, that the prospects for export were very bright indeed this year. The question I wish to ask him is this. I understand that three days ago at the dominion-provincial conference he said that export possibilities this year were much worse than they were last year. I wonder how he reconciles those two statements.

Mr. Chairman, I did not bother discussing all the details that have been raised today. I wanted the Leader of the Opposition back in the chamber before I made any further remarks. I do not like saying things in his absence; I like to talk right to him when making these points. But with regard to the question of the figures I would ask the committee to keep in mind that during the last four years the Liberals were in power they sold about 273 million bushels per year, on the average.
That is not an answer to the question I asked.
Second, during our period of office we exported about 321 million bushels per year in the last five years.
My figures do not show that.
If you look at the export outlook you will see that this year we expect to export 470 million bushels. Is that the figure the hon. member is talking about?
I have not got the actual figures before me; I have just the statement.

That is the figure. If you subtract the 140 million or 150 million bushels of domestic depletions in a good year, this means that even the very conservative people who are working in my department-the economists who do not like to go too far out on a limb-are predicting exports this year of 320 million to 330 million bushels. I do not make any predictions until near the end of the crop years, and then I like to zero in on the target as close as I can get.
When I say there is going to be tougher competition, I know there is. I simply say that with the government redoubling its efforts, even if other people come in there is nothing for us to fear; we can still handle all the grain grown in western Canada this year, even though it is one of the best crops on record.

Mr. Chairman, I take great pleasure in rising at this stage of our discussion on the revised estimates of the Department of Agriculture for 1962-63. Born into a farming family in Gaspe, a rural area where I practice my profession and where I am, thus, constantly in contact with the farmers, I suggest I am in a position to know their problems quite well.
During my short experience, I have noticed that the political parties, including the Social Credit party, of course, have been using a bit too much agriculture as a political football through the years. This tendency has shown itself to a greater extent these last few years and, as a new member in this house, I have been shocked by the remarks of our politicians on the subject since the beginning of this session. This tendency is worsening on the government side. When we hear the surprising and sometimes contradictory statements of the Minister of Agriculture, we wonder whether he is not nervous on account of the uncertainty prevailing among this minority and austerity government.
It seems that everything is said and done to get the electorate vote, but definitely not to improve conditions for the farming class. Mr. Chairman, I say that agriculture is too noble, too great and too important a sector of our economy to confuse it and drag it in the political ring.
I have already mentioned in this house, and I repeat it, that agriculture is the basis of our economy. Thus, if we want to insure the soundness of our economical structure, let us see to it first that the foundations are

sound, for a castle built up on sand will finally crumble down some day. In other words, a patchwork policy, a short term policy, can only endanger the very life of agriculture in our country. What we need, in Canada, is an over-all, new, sound and long term agricultural policy, a policy that could be developed in co-operation with the provinces, which are in a position to know more intimately and more closely the problems of their farmers.
Several good pieces of legislation have been adopted, both by previous administrations and by this one. However, several of them are of no or little use because they are difficult to apply, and others are not applicable, especially to the eastern farmers. Once again, I have nothing against the western farmers, and the eastern farmers have nothing against the western farmers. I wish to be clearly understood on that point. The treatment that the western farmers have had, and by which they have benefited, on certain occasions, must not be considered and, in fact, is not considered by the eastern farmers as a favour. They were entitled to it.
However, Mr. Chairman, it will be readily admitted, I hope, that the eastern farmers, in similar circumstances, have not received and do not receive a similar treatment. Certain laws, like the Crop Insurance Act for instance, apply only to grain. Now, as the western farmers are the greatest grain producers in Canada, they are the only ones at present to benefit from that legislation. Once again, there is nothing wrong in that. I think, and it is also the attitude of the party to which I have the honour to belong, that crop insurance should apply not gradually but concurrently to other farm products, in order that the eastern farmers may also take advantage of it. Our crops in the eastern part of the country and especially in the area I represent, are very often damaged or completely destroyed by bad weather, as is the case this year, both in Quebec and in the maritime provinces. In what situation are our farmers on account of such a disaster?
Since crop insurance does not cover the products and areas affected, farmers must face with apprehension not only winter, but also the sowing season, next spring. A national crop insurance scheme should be set up in our country, in conjunction with the provinces, so that all farmers, both from western and eastern Canada, may take advantage of the benefits of that legislation. I would greatly appreciate an increase both in the government's contribution of the pre-27507-3-1251

When I have finished my remarks. In addition, eastern farmers, in their efforts to improve their lot, increase their income and ensure the welfare of their families, are faced with obstacles and problems on all sides.
Because of his geographical situation, he happens to be far from centres supplying the grain he needs, whether for sowing purposes or to feed his cattle. This causes serious difficulties in our farm development. Western grain is very expensive, in spite of the assistance to shipping from the west to the east which, incidentally, was affected by the austerity program of the government.
For instance, if storage does not take place early in the fall, a price increase follows in the spring when that grain arrives at the elevators at the lakehead. Steps should be taken to ensure that western feed grain is shipped in sufficient amount to our eastern ports before the close of navigation in the fall. Here I completely agree with those who advocate and insist on the immediate construction of storage facilities in eastern Quebec, for instance, where our farmers could get supplies at any time at reasonable prices. It seems to me that the present western grain transport assistance policy should apply to wheat and other grain coming from Ontario and going east.
Of course, time does not allow to deal with all agricultural matters of importance, but let us consider for a moment the dairy industry. In my opinion, there is a lot to be done in that most important area for our eastern farmers and especially those in the province of Quebec, a lot more, in any case, than to tell our dairy farmers: "Cut down your dairy production, or we shall remove the subsidies", as the Minister of Agriculture said recently. At a time when everything should be done to stimulate our economy through various means, at a time when we are asked to look after agriculture, which is threatened, as the Catholic Farmers' Union recently pointed out, farmers are told to stop producing. We on this side of the house feel that the dairy industry, one of the most important we have, should receive special encouragement.
The promotion of consumption with regard to our dairy products, in their various forms, should be encouraged by every means of publicity at our disposal.

How many children, for instance, even in the wealthier families, do not drink enough milk when they go to school. The government should introduce a policy of free milk distribution in our schools. The health of our human capital, the strength of our young people-our leaders and workers of tomorrow-is more important and serious, I think, than niggardliness on account of austerity or on any pretext.
What we need in the farming field is, to my mind, information as well as commercial agencies which would revive our farm markets and, in many areas, create new ones.
