I am pleased to have this opportunity to stand up in support of one of the greatest ministers of agriculture this country has ever had. Certainly, in the past six months there has been plenty of evidence to support that contention. One could, if needed, go back two years. There is ample evidence already in the history books of what this man has done for Canadian agriculture right across Canada.
This debate began amid a great deal of interest and concern with regard to a speech which the minister made in Regina. The second speaker for the official opposition dropped the subject immediately after the minister had dealt with it so fully in the speech he finished a few minutes ago. Apparently the official opposition have had their fill of wheat sales and wheat exports.
[Mr. Bechard.)
Wait a while.

I hear someone say "wait a while". I am sure that with the energy they have over there and with the help of their research staff they will dig up some more muck and start to throw it. I am equally certain it will all be answered.
I am interested in this debate for two reasons, first, because when the debate began there was concern expressed about what the minister had said in Regina, and interest in the two propositions he had held out to the farmers and asked them to discuss in the winter months ahead. He asked them to consider the possibility of backing some of the credit risk in future sales, and he told them they might have difficulty in an expanding credit sales market, which is the situation in the world wheat market today. He told them that they might have difficulty keeping abreast with some of the credit sales made by other countries. That is evident because, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam suggested in his speech, Canada was perhaps lagging behind some other countries in credit sales. So I think that the minister was justified in expressing his conclusion that Canada needed to be prepared to move forward in the field of credit sales.
The minister stated that he wanted the farmers to understand the position clearly, and wanted them to consider the possibility of their taking a share in perhaps a credit risk. What did he suggest? He suggested two or three cents a bushel off the final payment on wheat. That is not a large amount which any farmer would immediately turn down. I am certain that the farmers of western Canada in particular want to pay their way and stand behind this country in its efforts to sell more wheat. What is so wrong with taking part of the credit risk to the tune of two or three cents a bushel? I would ask the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate this question. If this country, or this government, or even if his government, decided upon a fisheries exports sales policy and asked the fishermen to take a certain percentage, say one half or one quarter of a cent per pound, off their price of fish, would his fishermen not support that, if they knew that the government would stand the rest of the credit risk? Would his fishermen not be pleased to see the country move in to an aggressive export market in that product? I am sure that they would, in the same way that producers of other products besides fish and wheat would. This is evident under the

Export Credits Insurance Act which we have greatly enlarged, where the manufacturer already takes 15 per cent of the credit risk and the Export Credits Insurance Corporation stands the other 85 per cent. There is nothing wrong with the proposal as far as I can see. It is a proposal which enables the farmers to get behind this government, or any other government, in order to sell their products, and 1 am certain that anyone in business will appreciate the fact, that they are likely to pool their share of the load.
It is interesting to note some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Assiniboia. The minister dealt with them quite fully, but the hon. member has quite a record for coming out with famous words. We all remember his phrase "Peanuts". He said about the Chinese agreement that it was "lopsided". Now he calls this idea "fantastic", "incredible" and so on. These expressions are all quoted in the Regina Leader-Post.
I think the minister has pointed out the basis for this initial proposal and the soundness of it. If anyone is in doubt let him ask himself whether the lumbermen would not be interested in sharing part of the credit risks of a large credit sale-or the fisherman, or the fruit growers. I am certain that the major producers of any industry will be prepared to take two or three cents a bushel off their products in order to support this proposal fully. So therefore it is no wonder that on second thoughts we have had some of the about faces which we have seen here today. 1 realize that in a country like Canada we must be careful not to enter into a credit race with regard to needed products, but we must maintain our credit sales in order to hold our position in world markets. Canada is, of course, the largest commercial exporter of wheat in the world today. That is quite a position to hold for a country as sparsely populated as this one.
The hon. member for Red Deer spoke at great length about the areas which were untapped which we could still get into. Some knowledge of the wheat industry was portrayed by his party when another member of the same party asked what other countries we sell wheat to besides the United States and China. The minister replied that we sell wheat to 44 countries, that we are endeavouring to move into every country of the world with wheat sales. The minister stated in his speech in Regina the following, and I should like to read from the Western Producer:
However, Mr. Hamilton thought a great challenge to wheat sales lay in new and untapped markets. If, through international commodity agreements, newly developing nations could get stabilized floor prices for their own basic products, living standards would go up and with even the slightest increase a large market would be opened to Canada's grain.
Supply-Agriculture
This shows the interest and continual watchful eye which the minister has, and is continuing to have, on all the untapped markets which may exist in the world today.
The hon. member for Red Deer dealt at great length with the untapped markets still within what he termed the free world. He said that hunger and want were the greatest threat to peace in the world today. He classed that hunger threat over and above communism. He classed it over and above some of the other racial threats made in recent days. He classed hunger as the most important and dangerous threat in the world today. He went on to say that surplus food was our best weapon, and that we could use it. But he wanted integration with a defence policy, an external affairs policy, and an agricultural policy. Well, if that is not using food as a weapon of war, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said-that is the only point he made with which I agree-it is certainly the next thing to it. He must have meant that he wanted the external affairs department to put out literature for communist countries to read, so that they could be "red as well as fed". Perhaps that is what he had in mind.
In connecting his integrated system of defence, he must have had in mind the use of food, or use of the lack of food, as a weapon in this so-called cold war which is existing between east and west.
Do not misconstrue what he said.

I am quoting practically word for word and I am sure Hansard will bear me out. He went on to say that the communist system lent itself better than our free world system to the use of food and trading policies in their aggressive ideas. All this will be on Hansard without any doubt. But when he asked how we would get into these untapped areas-and the western farmers are always interested in furthering Canadian sales, which is the theme of this debate-the minister made a couple of suggestions, although some people did not like them. One idea for furthering sales, according to the hon. member for Red Deer, was to have a two price system. Many western members here have worked for a two price system. He used this as a method to get into untapped markets. He used it as a method to lower our external price and to raise, one might say, our internal price. What effect would that have on the world wheat market? What effect would it have on the international wheat agreement? A two price system to enable us to get into untapped markets would place Canadian wheat at a price on the world wheat market which would ruin the market

Supply-Agriculture
and ruin the international wheat agreement. There would just not be any agreement, and certainly alter a few years there would be a very highly subsidized agricultural industry in Canada, because our internal price would have to remain a great deal higher than that of the international market. There is one thing we must guard against as strongly as possible, the effect of lowering the international wheat market. If we ever start cutting prices, no one knows where it will end. Nothing could ruin the farmers more quickly than the cutting of the international wheat price.
He went on to deal at great length, as some Social Crediters are wont to do, with the starving people in the world today. He spoke of India and the starving people there.
I wonder whether the problems in India are not perhaps something besides food and the getting of food over there. It might be interesting to point out that India has the largest cattle population in the world today and that while many go hungry in that country there is still food available. However, other barriers exist which prohibit them from using it. There are other areas which could be developed to produce food and reduce some of the starving that goes on in the world today.
He talked at some length with regard to an international settlement account on which sales on the international market could be made and products would be then paid for under this international settlements account. I wonder whether printed money would be satisfactory on that international settlements account. I wonder how credit money would work in that regard, or how debt free money would work, or how their system of deficit financing would work. It would be very interesting to see them in operation.
The hon. member for Red Deer spoke also of another matter, and this is one point on which I agree with him. He said that in the agricultural field Canada itself is its best customer. I agree with him. Canada can and does consume practically all of its cattle, hogs and sheep, not all the butter but most of the milk and a large share of the grain. However, he went on to say that we should develop some way in which we could get the surplus grain in the west down to the less fortunate areas in the east. I hope he was not thinking of an earlier speech made here by one of his supporters with regard to the wheat board, when he said he wanted to buy wheat for a cent a pound in Quebec. He cannot buy it in western Canada for that price so I do not know how he could buy it in Quebec and cover the cost of hauling it down. I do not know who would sell it to him.

Anyway, it was interesting to hear his theories on China and how we should not be selling wheat to China but should be selling to some other areas. The minister dealt quite fully with the question as to who is selling to China and who is not, and whether other countries have stopped, and whether we are the only commonwealth country that is trading with that nation. Certainly I believe that we must watch the conditions that exist in India and China. However, up to the present time other commonwealth countries are trading with China and we should perhaps continue with our trading policy either until the situation worsens or China announces an aggressive policy under which it could perhaps take over all of India, which as yet it has not done.
The Leader of the Opposition made a very interesting speech. The hon. member for Bow River placed a question before him; he did not answer. He set about reading something vaguely, but he did say that the minister's remarks in Regina were ridiculous. This was his statement on November 14, as reported in Hansard. I listened closely for any constructive ideas that might have come from the Leader of the Opposition. He was great at criticizing but he offered no solutions. He suggested his $2 a bushel price for wheat was a great thing. Actually he pointed out that it would be a subsidized price. I do not know how his other supporters, particularly those who feel that eastern Canada may be running a little bit short, would like that. Anyway he thought that the $2 a bushel price was a good idea. He spoke at length with regard to how he thought the United States trade policy was a good one. Actually if he read the papers here recently he would know that the United States said to the European common market, "You trade with us, or else. If you raise tariffs on our goods we will have to do the same with goods from your country". That is not much of a free trade attitude. He said we must give the European common market a great big push forward. He said we must protect the producers of this country, that they are going to have to adjust to the European common market, even if they have to adjust their production. That is a dangerous thing he was dealing with.
The Prime Minister of this country sought the assurance of Great Britain that our producers would have the same privileges in that market as we have today. That assurance was given, for which we are very thankful. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam worried a great deal about the risk. He was suspicious; he was worried. I am sure he used the word "suspicious" about four times. He also went on to say that he had to admit that other

countries were expanding their credit sales and that Canada had not actually touched on credit sales as yet. However, he was worried that the farmers were going to have to stand two cents a bushel on wheat sales. Apparently he feels that the fact that the farmers are asked to spend two cents to three cents a bushel is a great big risk to future wheat credit sales. Yet he contradicted himself in his own remarks when he said this was an assured market, that Canada had not touched the bottom of the barrel with regard to credit sales. I listened very closely to his remarks in order to see whether he was against the two suggestions in the minister's Regina speech. From his remarks I gathered that he was worried and suspicious about it, but he did not know whether he was against it any more, and he did not know whether he was for it. He was just worried.
He ought to be.
You cannot really blame him for being worried; that is true. Anybody who left his native province under the conditions under which he left it.
He did not leave; he was chased out.

I bow to the hon. member's knowledge.
The minister tells us his second proposal with regard to the wheat board and the actions of the wheat board. He pointed out that there were very few people who were so eager to condemn him who knew what they were condemning. This is borne out in a report published in a weekly news analysis featuring farm policy where we find the following:
Farm organizations and members of parliament demonstrated this week how little they understand the key farm problems. They also demonstrated how little they value the efforts of a minister who has accomplished so much for farmers in his two years in office.
That is what this farm weekly analysis said with regard to some of the most eager critics of the minister's Regina speech. Actually the minister pointed out that the wheat board handled the wheat and offered the wheat to the grain exchange to sell at such and such a price on a given day. The grain exchange consists of a body of agents who are prepared to sell it at that set price which the wheat board lays down on that given day. The minister's idea was that we should have a national organization specifically interested in furthering Canadian sales at home and abroad.
Certainly the idea has been discussed for some time. Certainly the idea has a great deal of merit. The wheat pools and the

United Grain Growers admitted that they are and have been considering it. They think they might like to enter into the plan but it is a big step to take, as the minister warned them. He said he knew they had a knowledge of the trade and would proceed very cautiously and properly, though he hoped that eventually they would take this step so that competition in the sale of grain could be increased and more grain sold and, so that no corner of this country and no corner of the world would be left untouched as the result of an aggressive sales policy for western wheat.

I can say I had a striking example of this as a young boy. Besides, when we refer to Hansard for March 1957, at which time his party was in power, we realize that the then Liberal ministers had the same headaches as the Conservatives today. That is why we say that under the two old parties, "the more things change, the more they are the same."
Mr. Chairman, I should like, at the offset, to give a few details concerning the pamphlets which we are trying to get. Last week, for example, we asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) for a French version of the folders published by the Canadian wheat board. In fact, I wish to inform the minister that, as far as I am concerned, I am ready

to use Shakespeare's tongue as soon as he will consent to speak in French. And, as a proof of my good will, I say in this house that I shall be happy each time that co-operation will be given to bring about national understanding in our country. Each time I put forward a claim for the French language, I want to show that in our parliament in Ottawa you have to ask to get something. I find each day that our brothers from western Canada were unaware of the fact that we were sometimes discriminated against, especially during the 22 years of Liberal government, which has done nothing to promote understanding between the two races.
Apparently, nothing could be done about it, save to accept the situation.
Thus, there is nothing surprising in the fact that everything has to be done in the field of national understanding.
As an equal partner in Canada, I even want to challenge the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) and tell him that, as soon as he has learned to speak French, I shall speak English, and we shall both go and visit Lili St. Cyr and Maurice Richard, to recall his famous statement. He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the third or fourth year in a row in which I have introduced this particular bill. We have had debates on it on other occasions, one of which lasted a full day during the time when the rules of the house were such that private members' business could be dealt with for a full day. One of the theories which was supposed to be of assistance to the general public, in so far as the operation of free enterprise is concerned, was that free enterprise would be guided by the principle of competition; that this would automatically bring to the

consuming public the best quality product at the lowest possible price. But this theory or principle, so-called, of competition has not operated too well, if at all-at least during the time I have been alive, and I am sure for many years before I was born.
The business community soon discovered that price and quality competition amongst themselves was not too helpful to business, so they very quickly dispensed with the operation of competition in so far as price and quality were concerned and moved into the field of price fixing arrangements and restrictions so far as quantity, quality of production and the like, were concerned. They found this to be far more profitable than competition in the field of price and quality. Competition was very quickly confined almost exclusively to the field of advertising. Advertising media were used to convince the general public that it was getting a better quality product and the lowest possible priced product, when in fact that was not the case. This practice still operates today. We are still told that Gleem or Glush, or whatever other type of toothpaste one might want to use, is the best type of toothpaste for making your teeth whitest, your breath sweetest, and to make you sexually attractive to somebody else. This is what advertising tells us. It does not at all produce a better quality product or a lowest possible priced product; it merely attempts to convince us that such is the case.
Trading stamps fall within the category of being an advertising gimmick, in that they are used to try to convince the consuming public that it is getting something for nothing, that these stamps are in fact free. Perhaps this is social credit in operation; I do not know. But it is a known fact that somehow or other the business which uses these trading stamps, whichever one it might be, has to find the money to provide the stamps and the articles for which the stamps are traded. The cost of these articles comes from the sales dollar of the particular business or company, and the consumer pays for the trading stamps and for the articles he receives through the prices he pays for the commodities themselves. Notably, and almost exclusively, these trading stamps are used in that section of the business community which is engaged in selling food products.
The use of trading stamps, besides being dishonest and contributing to the cost of food, tends to contribute a great deal to the concentration of economic power into fewer and fewer hands within whatever section of the business community the stamps are used. The corner grocery, for a variety of reasons, is not able to afford the type of advertising budget which will allow him to compete in the

Criminal Code
advertising field with chain stores using stamps. These corner grocery stores tend to suffer as a consequence. In fact, the royal commission on price spreads of food products indicated in its report-I would just like to make a brief reference to some of the statistics contained in it-that 37.2 per cent of the business accrued to food chain stores in 1951 while in 1958 this had increased to 64 per cent. On the other hand, in 1951, while independent grocers, corner grocery stores and the like, had 62.8 of the market, by 1958 this had declined to 36 per cent. I am sure that any analysis of the statistics beyond 1958 will show that this has grown even more out of proportion and that food chain stores have an even larger percentage of the market, while the independent grocers or small corner grocery stores have a relatively smaller percentage.
This growth of economic power and control has been undoubtedly enhanced by the use of trading stamp plans to the point where the consuming public is relatively helpless, to the point where the farmer himself-about whom there was some discussion earlier this afternoon-gets caught within the squeeze by virtue of vertical integration and the like, and to the point where the small businessman finds himself in difficulties. This growth of economic dictatorship, assisted and contributed to by the use of trading stamps and other similarly dishonest methods of advertising, puts these three basic elements of our society in an unfair and helpless position, namely the consumer, the farmer and the small businessman. I think the only element in society which can protect these individuals is parliament.
The Criminal Code of Canada has had in it since 1905 a prohibition against the use of trading stamps. However this law which was enacted 57 years ago has a loophole in it. It says in effect that you cannot issue or use trading stamps, but the loophole is that you can in some instances. That is why stores such as Loblaws and the like are able to issue trading stamps. The intent of the particular bill before us is to plug that loophole and make effective the principle contained in the law, namely that trading stamps should not be used. So long as the government in office-and the previous government allowed this to happen-wants to maintain the present section 322 of the Criminal Code we will continue to at least give lip service to the concept that trading stamps are harmless and are not disastrous to our economy. I think this parliament should persist in this matter and extend the principle contained in that section so that trading stamps are completely outlawed. This bill merely seeks to make the law effective and to block the loophole which
has been found by trading stamp companies and by food chain stores, thereby providing the protection necessary to retail firms, consumers and small businessmen.

Having listened to the hon. member for Skeena discuss once again the subject of trading stamps,
I have to agree he deserves a certain amount of credit for his perseverance and assiduity. He has brought this subject forward, he reminded us, for four years and I think he shows considerable tenacity. Although the bill before the house contains a few proposals which are neither new nor original, they are interesting and might well be timely.
There is nothing very new about trading stamps, either, because they have been used in one form or another for over 60 years. The practice of giving stamps, coupons or other devices, while usually recognized as legitimate and confining itself to a certain section of the market, seem to have a tendency to move in cycles, that is, it develops and recedes. The present situation has developed through the activities of the promoters of trading stamps, over which the retailer has little control, and the problem which confronts the consumer is whether or not trading stamps have the result of increasing the price of the goods he buys. It is generally agreed that this is the case. It seems also that promoters and distributors are the people who favour the system of distributing trading stamps, and benefit most from it.
When we examine this whole situation we find that the use of trading stamps is actually an inducement to buy and that these trading stamps are then placed in the realm of advertising, which automatically opens up a wide field for discussion. However, let me point out that there is considerable difference between legitimate advertising and a type of promotion scheme to suggest to the buyer he is getting something for nothing. Obviously the cost involved in the distribution and promotion of trading stamps is considerable and it is equally obvious that somewhere along the line the consumer will be paying. In many cases where we are subjected to the advertising of stamps, the costs must be computed. In spite of what can be said against this practice there are those who collect trading stamps with considerable enthusiasm and would feel that government interference would be an imposition and a violation of some of their rights.
At the same time the practice of issuing trading stamps has been opposed by various organizations as a drain on time, effort and money and definitely not in the best interests of the consumer.

Criminal Code
However, if the consumer concerned wishes action taken, it must be admitted that his protests so far have been erratic and divided and that the amending of the Criminal Code does seem to be rather a harsh manner in which to curb what some believe to be an innocuous practice. On the other hand, it may take such action to dispel the illusion that the consumer is getting something for nothing.
In essence, the bill seems to fail in its basic intent in that it proposes a form of regimentation, to replace freedom of choice in human conduct by government regulatory action.
In application the bill would prevent the retailer from supplying a piece of paper representing the retailer's intention to redeem it by way of premiums on purchases. Surely this would inhibit only one field of merchandising, and if it was the intention of the trade to give discount or premium on goods purchased, many other avenues could be opened for such action. The interception of business transactions is certainly not the prerogative of government, and legislation should not be substituted for freedom of choice. While the bill does try to achieve something constructive it appears to be right in principle but wrong in practice, and I regret I cannot support it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the bill before the house in the name of the hon. member for Skeena. This measure proposes that the Criminal Code be amended to prevent the use of trading stamps by corporations engaged in the sale of food in supermarkets and the like. Of course, as those of us in this party believe, such a measure is badly needed in Canada today when trading stamps are being so widely used in order to induce people to buy goods they do not need with money which so often they require for other purposes. The use of trading stamps is one of the bad features of what has been called our acquisitive society.
There is prevalent in commercial circles the view that it is the citizen's duty to consume whatever may be produced by the industrial machine. Decisions regarding consumption do not really therefore rest with the consumer; they rest in the hands of those who control the economy of this country. The consumer is not the proud possessor of what economists call the consumer's sovereignty. His sovereignty, if he has any, is hedged about by the blandishments and inducements that are forced upon him by the advertising industry. If advertising will not induce him to consume the things produced by industry then, so their philosophy goes, he can be induced to consume these things by offering him trading stamps which entitle him to small prizes that become obtainable if he has accumulated enough trading stamps. Much of the industrial activity today is geared to the production of goods which are often a duplication of goods which have already been produced by other manufacturers. There is such tremendous duplication and overlapping that the great concentration of advertising today has resulted.
Let us consider the example of toothpaste. The hon. member for Skeena referred to toothpastes called Gleem and Glush, describing them as two well known brands. I think the house will be interested in knowing that the cost of an ordinary tube of toothpaste consists to the extent of 50 per cent,

in the actual cost of manufacturing the tube and the toothpaste, and getting it to the shelves of the merchant, while the other 50 per cent of the cost consists of advertising.
Of course, one brand of toothpaste is just the same as another. There are practically no differences between them. They all make extravagant claims. The people who have studied the subject tell us that only one brand has any justification whatever for the extravagant claims which all of them are making. Because I do not wish to give any one manufacturer an undue advantage I will refrain from mentioning the name of that particular brand which, so we are told, has some slight justification for the extravagant claims made on its behalf. But this is typical of our situation today.
We are spending far too much money on things which have little or no social value, while we are neglecting things which are badly needed. We are spending millions of dollars on advertising; and of course trading stamps are a form of advertising. Their purpose is the same, namely to induce the consumer to buy things which he may very well have no desire to buy. In fact, the suggestion has been put forward in some quarters that there ought to be a tax on advertising. No doubt members of this house at an appropriate time will be able to give consideration to such a proposal. At any rate, I congratulate the hon. member for Skeena on putting forward this bill which I know will commend itself to members of all parties. I know they will be anxious to restrict their comments upon it so that the vote can be called before the hour for private members' business this afternoon has expired. I am sure all of them will join me in congratulating the hon. member on placing this bill before the house.
I should like to conclude by suggesting that, as the hon. member for Skeena himself said in presenting the bill to the house, legislation of this kind is badly needed not only in the field of trading stamps but in many other fields. We must put an end to false and misleading advertising. We must put an end to false and misleading methods of merchandising. I suggest to hon. members and to you, Mr. Speaker, that the house can make a good beginning by passing this bill unanimously this afternoon.

Yes, I think I can agree with that-we are not troubled with trading stamps. Saskatchewan has a law respecting trading stamps which is condemned pretty strongly by many small businessmen engaged in private enterprise in that province. They feel it is a weapon held over their heads. This may or may not be true. But I think it is evident in this country and in the
United States that people are looking for less and less government interference. They are seeking less and less control. We saw this in the recent election in the United States. The states are continually complaining about the federal government moving into their field.
The same is evident in Canada. The provinces are continually worried and complaining about the federal government moving into their field of jurisdiction. One can also go back to the municipalities which are worried and complaining about the provincial governments taking over their responsibilities. In fact, to take it one step further, one can go back to the people who are worried about the municipalities taking away what one might call some of their opportunities for free choice.
Stamp plans have been around for a long time and we have seen many different versions of them. Someone said that we have had these stamps around for the last 65 years. I know they have been in Nabob coffee and tea for a long time. Certainly when I was a little boy, growing up, and opened the kitchen cupboard there were generally a few Nabob stamps there. People used to save box tops from packages of cereals, which is much the same thing, possibly to get toy water guns in those days. I forget what we used the box tops for but we thought the cereal was pretty good. In fact, manufacturers of soaps and cereals use all kinds of gimmicks, such as 10-cent coupons inside the box.
It came out in the price spreads commission inquiry that manufacturers of cereals were perhaps the greatest users of advertising gimmicks and give-aways at that time. In fact, the commission went to great lengths to establish that the cereal industry was perhaps the greatest user of coupons inside the boxes or the idea of saving box tops in order to get something, all for the purpose of trying to get customers to buy the particular product.
How widespread is this practice? We must determine first whether or not it is of such great importance that the federal government should take action. I have looked at some statistics and referred to previous debates. A survey made in 1959 indicated that 59 per cent of the people of Canada saved trading stamps in those areas where they were offered. These stamps are widely used in the province of Quebec, and in that province 80 per cent of the people saved them and patronized stores that give stamps. Whether it is right or wrong, the people are saving them and using them.
There is the question of whether or not 80 per cent of the people of Quebec can be

Criminal Code
wrong. We may have had some doubts recently whether they are wrong or right in their views, but we must still give them a reasonable amount of credit for being able to judge whether or not they are doing something wrong that is going to harm them and put them in debt, or cost them more money. It is quite an impressive figure when one realizes that 80 per cent of the people in one province where stamps are available save and make use of them. It is also quite impressive that 59 per cent of the people in Canada generally do the same thing.
I come from a rural area and I know that even if trading stamps were lawful in Alberta they would probably not play a very big part in my riding, because we have no large city in the riding and there is no massive amount of trade carried on in one large city. Therefore I am perhaps not aware of the direct evils of this very vicious scheme being carried on by the trading stamp companies. Some of the people who are opposed to trading stamps suggest that the 59 per cent of the people of Canada who use them are not intelligent enough to know when they are being fooled. They suggest that these people become bewildered counting stamps and save them but forget to use them, and so on. They suggest that people who save stamps buy things they do not really need, that they become confused about the value of the goods they buy, that they are dazzled by the advertising in Ottawa, for example, of such stores as Loblaws, where trading stamps are given.
These people who are opposed to the idea think that the people who make use of trading stamps are actually being fooled into thinking that they are getting something for nothing, when they actually are getting nothing and are paying for everything they get. Some of the opponents of this scheme suggest that only those who are in the business of distributing stamps and the goods that the stamps will purchase are in favour of the plan. In my view the fact that 80 per cent of the people of Quebec and 59 per cent of the people of Canada use them suggests that perhaps a fair number of people support the idea of trading stamps.
It might be interesting to refer to my experience on first coming to Ottawa. My wife was soon made aware by neighbours on our street of the fact that she had better deal here or there because this or that store gave away trading stamps and had good premiums. I do not know whether my wife really saved them, but I know that our neighbours in that area certainly did and some of them were not getting stung on what they were purchasing with these stamps.

Actually the matter boils down to the old saying, if I may take hon. members back to the farm for a minute, that you can lead a horse to water but you can't make him drink. This is perhaps very true with regard to trading stamps. You can bring in legislation and force these companies not to issue trading stamps, but will this stop the practice of enticing people to shop at a particular store? Will this do away with box top premiums and all the other gimmicks that advertising men are paid to dream up to try to get around the laws that this and other bodies pass? This is the question.
The hon. member who moved second reading of the bill suggested that there was a loophole in the act, and possibly there might be. But can the loophole be successfully plugged when there is such a wide advertising appeal to various types of customers? I wonder about this point. If the loophole cannot be plugged, and assuming that the people think that it is not right to plug it because they are participating in the scheme, maybe we should not pass the bill at all. I have no really strong objections one way or the other, but there are several question I must ask myself before I am prepared to say that we should blindly accept and pass the bill just because trading stamps have been talked about for 65 years. As the bill suggests, at various times they have been covered under the Criminal Code and at other times not. The bill suggests that perhaps at one time the loophole was plugged but the provision was deleted in 1953 and 1954. I did not have time to look up the debates then and I might not have time to give the house the benefit of my research on the debates in 1953 and 1954, but why was the provision deleted then? That is an interesting question which has gone unanswered so far in this debate. I should like to know the reaction of the house at that time.
What do trading stamps actually do? What are they? If prices are not increased, they are in a sense a discount. I think even the mover of the bill would admit that if prices do not increase they are in a sense a discount to the purchaser of a certain commodity. We are told these stamps represent a discount of something like 2 per cent or 2J per cent on a merchant's gross sales. Actually, I think a strong argument could be presented to show that stamps increase competition. They tend to draw customers from one store to another. This is, perhaps, the sole reason they are used so extensively.
Well, Mr. Speaker, is competition so great that we do not want it increased? Is competition a wrong thing to have between large companies? It has been my complaint in the

last few years that competition has not been keen enough, that some of these large companies tend to follow one another in the setting of prices. I immediately think of the farm machinery inquiry we had a few years ago. In that field one company set the price and others followed right behind. Certainly, there is great scope in dealing with any problem.
The question I am asking here is, do trading stamps not increase competition amongst the larger stores? If they do, is this wrong? This question has gone unanswered so far in this debate. Do we want to see less competition between the larger stores today? Certainly, I want to see more competition because the keener the competition the better the service I am apt to receive as a customer and the better price I am apt to get as a customer. This has been my experience. If that thought is wrong, then certainly there are many things wrong with the trend of thought amongst the economists.
The question might be asked, do trading stamps increase the cost of the commodity we wish to buy? Has it been successfully proven that trading stamps do increase the cost of the products we buy? We have areas in Canada where trading stamps are not allowed and areas where they are allowed. Can it be proven, by looking at the cost of living index for any city in which trading stamps are used extensively that the cost of living is higher than for a city where trading stamps are not allowed? A very interesting comparison could be drawn if such figures could be obtained. Certainly, such a comparison would prove conclusively whether or not trading stamps are evil and should be ruled out by the passage of this particular bill.
As I mentioned before, there are rural areas and perhaps other areas situated many miles from the large chain stores which would not be affected a great deal by this particular problem. However, we must still have an interest in all things that affect the products we need to purchase in order to maintain the living standard we have and of which we think so much. Actually, there is a very interesting brief written by Eugene Beem, entitled "Who Profits From Trading Stamps?". I should like to quote from part of it:
If vendors do not raise their prices when they adopt stamps, consumers enjoy a discount through premiums merchandise equivalent to about 2 per cent to 21 per cent of their stamp store purchases. The typical premium value is about $2.45 per 1,000 stamps, based on a study of the catalogues of ten representative stamp companies and the prices of a large northern California department store. (At discount house prices the value is about 18 per cent lower.)
Business of the House
He goes on to give an idea of the effect they have on prices. I could read from this brief at great length. The author even suggests in this particular chapter that prices are reduced. It is suggested that price reductions may be even spurred. The data gathered by the bureau of labour is a clear indication that stamps have not forced up food prices in general. In fact, this data suggests that stamps may have held down price increases. The author goes on to deal with this thought that stamps may have a tendency to hold down prices. This could be a fact, if one could prove whether or not they are actually increasing competition or decreasing competition.
I believe the question boils down to whether or not we consider profits are wrong. A great deal has been said of late in respect of profits, and opinions have been changing.
I suggest that companies using trading stamps are, in a sense, like giant co-operatives. You are paid dividends in direct relationship to the value of the goods you purchase from the co-operatives. As everyone knows, if you do a certain amount of business with a co-operative you are paid dividends in direct relationship to the amount of business you do.
The question here is, who receives the profit? In so far as co-operatives are concerned, profits are distributed to their consumers. In so far as chain stores are concerned, they naturally keep the profits and distribute them to their shareholders. This procedure is considered all right in most countries, and certainly by most of the parties in this house. In so far as trading stamps are concerned, the stores are distributing dividends to their customers in direct relationship to the amount of goods those customers purchase. If we consider profits are not wrong, then we should allow a company to make a profit, as long as consideration is given to seeing that this profit is not too large. I suggest that, perhaps-
